div.p: THE eighth book of Suetonius' Lives of the Caesars contains his account of the three Flavian emperors, and this first chapter is a general introduction to the whole, giving (1) an estimate of the dynasty, (2) an account of its ancestry. The life of Vespasian proper begins with c. 2 Vespasianus natus est; cf. Titus...natus est (Tit. 1), Domitianus natus est (Dom. 1).
§ 1. sine ullis maiorum imaginibus: used of a man none of whose ancestors have held curule office, i. e. have attained the rank of aedile. See Cicero, Verrines, 5. 14. 36.
§ 2. T. Flavius Petro. His wife's name was Tertulla (c. 2). We know no more of him than Suetonius tells us, but he must have been a very old man at the time of Vespasian's birth, if alive at all.

p.note: . Reate (Rieti) was a town in Sabine territory on the Avens (Velino), at the point where the Via Salaria crossed the river. An inscription records that it was a praefectura in 27 B.C. (CIL. ix. 4677 = Dessau 6543). It did not become a municipium until imperial times (CIL. ix. 4686), so that Suetonius reference is anachronistic. Vespasian later settled some of his discharged veterans there (e.g. CIL. ix. 4684 = Dessau 2460).

: i.e. a time-expired veteran re-engaged by a military commander. He would be given charge of small bodies of recruits, and might thus come to be spoken of loosely also as a centurion. Or the qualification may only mean that Suetonius was uncertain of his rank.
: i.e. honesta missio, without which Petro could not have secured the usual praemia.
: i. e. his profession was the collecting of debts at a commission.
: Vespasian's father; we know nothing more of him. From the nature of his career (including the rumour that he had been a primipilaris), it seems probable that he was an eques.

. This was the portorium (harbourdues), which in Asia and Gaul was a tax of 20 per cent.; for other customs-districts cf. Hirschfeld, Kaiserliche Verwaltungsbeamten², pp. 79-80. That the rapacity of the 'farmers' was a byword (cf. Tac. Ann. 13. 50) is well shown by this passage; at a later period it led to the establishment of imperial procurators to supervise them.

div.p: § 3. faenus... exercuit: i.e. he was a moneylender. ...

p.note: . To her has been attributed an inscription found on the site of a house at Spoletium, in which something (presumably a statue) is dedicated to the emperor Gaius by a Polla (CIL. xi. 4778). Bormann (in Arch. Ep. Mitth. aus Oest., 1892, p. 33) points out that it is very unusual for such statues to be set up in private houses, and that where it was done some particular reason for gratitude may be assumed. He goes on to suggest that if this lady were our Vespasia Polla, as fits in with (1) the locality, (2) the symmetry, of the inscription; a motive for the dedication is at once given by the desire of Vespasia to win favour for her son's advancement, corresponding to Vespasian's own thanks in the Senate (c. 2). But the evidence for this attribution seems scanty: Spoletium after all is not Nursia, nor is Polla (a variant of Paulla) an uncommon name.
. Vespasia Polla had three children, but the eldest, a girl, died within the year (c. 5).

. Since Vespasian's brother is not mentioned by name again in the Life, though he is referred to on more than one occasion (cc. 2, 4, 5), some account of his career may be here given. Our chief authorities are the obituary notice in Tacitus : quinque et triginta stipendia in re publica fecerat, domi militiaeque clarus. innocentiam iustitiamque eius non argueres ; sermonis nimius erat: id unum septem annis quibus Moesiam, duodecim quibus praefecturam urbis obtinuit, calumniatus est rumor. (Hist. 3. 75), and a mutilated dedicatory inscription restored as follows:... [leg. divi Claudi pro pr. provin[c. Moe\siae, cur. census] Gallici, praef. urb[i | iterum (or tertium). Huic] senatus auctor[e | | imp. Caes. Vespasiano fratre | [clupeum posuit vadimon[is | honoris causa dilatis, [funus censorium] censuit, statuam | in forlo divi Augusti [ponen dam decrevit] (CIL. vi. 31293 = Dessau 984). We know also that he served on his brother's staff (ὑποστρατηγοῦντά oἱ) in Britain in 43 (Dio 60. 20). The chief difficulty of his career lies in his tenure of the praefectura urbis. The twelve years specified by Tacitus takes us back to 57, and this would fit well with the supposition that he succeeded L. Volusius Saturninus, who died in office in 56 (Tac. Ann. 13. 30; Plin. N. H. 7. 62). Unfortunately we know that L. Pedanius Secundus was assassinated by one of his slaves while praefectus urbi in 61 (Tac. Ann. 14. 42), and consequently it has been proposed to change the duodecim of Tacitus to septem or totidem (see Borghesi, Œuvres, iii, p. 327). But since there is at least one gap in Sabinus' tenure-Galba (who feared Vespasian) displaced him in favour of A. Ducenius Geminus (Tac. Hist. 1. 14) in 68, and he was only restored by Otho (Plut. Oth. 5; Tac. Hist. 1. 46), it is possible, though the matter must be left uncertain, that there was a second gap, for reasons unknown, in 60-61, and that the MS. reading of Tacitus is correct. At any rate, the suggested cursus below shows that the chronology of his career does not disallow this assumption. The thrilling story of Sabinus' negotiations with Vitellius on his brother's behalf after the second battle of Bedriacum, and his death after the conflagration of the Capitol, is given in Tacitus (Hist. 3. 64-74). He had at any rate children (Tac. Hist. 3. 69): we know of two sons, Flavius Sabinus (Suet. Dom. 10; Dio 65. 17), and Flavius Clemens (Suet. Dom. 15; Dio 67. 14), both put to death by Domitian. His wife's name is unknown: for a conjecture as to her identity and other matters connected with the family, see Edmundson, The Church in Rome in the First Century, Appendix D. I suggest the following dates for the cursus of Sabinus: Born Quaestor Praetor In Britain Consul 8 circa. 34 38 circa. 43 44-47 Governor of Moesia 48-54 circa. 69-34 = 35 years of public service ascribed to him by Tacitus. At any rate before his brother (51). Allusions of Tacitus to his superior standing (Hist. 3. 65, 75) would be absurd were this not so. He must have been a consular before holding this position (see S. E. Stout, The Governors of Moesia, p. 10 sq.). Curator of Gallic census 54-56 Praefectus urbi 56-60 4 years Praefectus urbi iterum 61-68 = 7 years Praefectus urbi tertium 69 = 1 year 12 years Put to death by 69 (December 19th). Vitellius' army
. Nursia (Norcia) was a mountain town in the Sabine country on a tributary of the Nar (Nera).

. His positions of tribunus militum and praefectus castrorum show that he was of the equestrian order, and a tried soldier of long standing. His son Vespasius was no doubt given the latus clavus by Augustus.

, about twenty miles from Nursia. It was in Umbria (but Nursia being quite cut off from other Sabine towns by the hills, and on the Umbrian side of the watershed, its natural outlet was down the valley of the Nar, near which Spoletium stood). It was here also that the supposed remains of Vespasia Polla's house were found (see above).

. Bormann (loc. cit.) suggests that this may possibly be the genitive of the noun, 'a place known as Vespasia's', i. e. Vespasia Polla's, but agrees that it is more probably the nominative of the adjective, tabernae or some such word being understood. We gather that the Vespasii were an old Italian family, as well as a distinguished one, and that the elder Sabinus made a good match.

div.p: § 4. e regione Transpadana. This was of course a disparaging report: 'Vespasian's great-grandfather was not even an Italian'. The whole chapter, and especially this last sentence, is evidence of careful independent research by Suetonius. Vespasian's descent is therefore as follows: supposed manceps operarum = uxor Reatina T. Flavius Petro = Tertulla Flavius Sabinus Vespasius Pollio Vespasia Polla praetorius puella T. Flavius Sabinus T. Flavius Vespasianus

§ 1. Vespasianus. Titus Flavius Vespasianus was his full name before he became emperor-it occurs in the inscription recording his arbitration in a boundary dispute (CIL. vi. 1268): every Flavius of this line whose praenomen is recorded is a Titus. His cognomen is obviously derived from his mother's gentilicium, a customary method in imperial times of naming the second son of a marriage (see Cagnat, Cours d'épigraphie latine, ed. 3, p. 66); similarly Domitian, from his mother Domitilla, though here it is the cognomen that was used.

p.note: . Only mentioned in this connexion by Suetonius: other writers speak more loosely of Reate as Vespasian's birthplace. Falacrinae (there are several alternative spellings of the name) was some twenty miles beyond Reate up the Avens valley, situated on the Via Salaria just before the crossing of the Apennines. The name seems to be preserved to-day in the Church of S. Silvestro in Falacrino, in the neighbourhood of Cività Reale.

: i. e. late in the day on November 17th, A.D. 9-the date is confirmed by the calendar of Philocalus (CIL. i², p. 255). Suetonius usually gives the year of a Caesar's birth either by the names of the consuls or by reference to some historical event connected with it: in only one other case (that of Tiberius) does he make use of both.
: the wife therefore of Flavius Petro: she must have been many years younger than her husband (cf. c. 5).
. Presumably this would be during the absence of Vespasian's father apud Helvetios. Cosa was an ancient town on the sea-coast of Etruria.

div.p: § 2. Sumpta virili toga: the coming-of-age ceremony among the Romans, taking place at about the age of sixteen. It was then that the boy would decide on his future career. ..

p.note: . The latus clavus, i. e. a broad purple stripe on the toga, was the recognized sign that the wearer belonged to the ordo senatorius, and was eligible for the public magistracies. Sons of senators assumed it ipso facto, and it would be conferred by the emperor-in this case by Tiberius-upon the sons of other wealthy and distinguished men as a qualification for a senatorial cursus. Vespasian then did not decide upon his career until later than usual; though the diu of Suetonius can at most mean two or three years, since Vespasian was praetor at the earliest possible age (see below), and probably quaestor not more than a year in excess of it. The tendency of Suetonius (and of Tacitus as well: cf. Hist. 3. 65, 75) to exaggerate Vespasian's undistinguished early career, making it forced on him almost against his own will, and especially unpromising in comparison with the career of Sabinus (who after all was probably only quaestor at the same age as Vespasian, i. e. one year above the minimum-see note on c. 1), may be attributed to the desire to find in his rise to power another ludibrium rerum mortalium, such as they had traced in that of Claudius.

: originally the slave who walked in front of his master to clear a way, then usually the client who performed a somewhat similar duty for his patron; e.g. Martial calls himself tumidi anteambulo regis = patron (2. 18). No doubt this is the sense in which Vespasia's 's taunt should be understood.

div.p: § 3. Tribunatum militum: an office held by young men before the quaestorship, with a view to giving them some experience of military affairs; they were known as tribuni laticlavii and would have no connexion with such a tribunus militum as Vespasius Pollio. Thrace was not at this time (the last years of Tiberius) a Roman province: it was a client kingdom, the king supported by a Roman resident magistrate with troops (see Tac. Ann. 2. 67).

p.note: . One of the quaestors of the year was usually allocated by lot to the governor of each of the senatorial provinces, and served him normally as financial overseer. The most probable date for Vespasian's quaestorship seems to be 35 (see below).

. The aedilitas and the tribunatus were alternative stages in the cursus honorum. In this office Vespasian incurred the anger of Gaius for his neglect of the streets of Rome (c. 5, and Dio 59. 12). According to the chronology of Dio his aedileship was in 38; his quaestorship therefore was probably in 35, for (1) in the absence of evidence to the contrary we may assume that the usual year's interval would elapse between his tenure of one and his candidature for the other; (2) his first candidature for the aedileship failed.

. The coniuratio referred to as occurring during Vespasian's term of office must be the revolt of Lentulus Gaetulicus, governor of Upper Germany, and Aemilius Lepidus, the emperor's brother-in-law. Sacrifices are recorded in the Acts of the Arval Brothers on 27th October: ob detecta nefaria con[silia in C. Caes. Aug. Germanicum Cn. Lentuli Gae[tulici] (Henzen, p. xlix), and that this was 27th October 39 is clear from the fact that Gaius was in Germany at the time of the revolt (Suet. Claud. 9), and that by 31st August 40 (the other possible year) he was back in Rome (Suet. Cal. 49). Vespasian therefore was praetor in 39, at the earliest possible age (thirty), and in the year immediately following his aedileship: this argues that he already possessed influential patronage.
: i. e. in the last place of all (there were six aediles). This passage is interesting as showing that there was still some reality in the magisterial elections in the Senate.
. Bentley's correction of the ac of the MSS. It is obvious that an antithesis to illam is required.

. See Suetonius Cal. 43 sq.: this was what Tacitus calls the Gaianarum expeditionum ludibrium (Hist. 4. 15; cf. Germ. 37). The fact that the campaign was undertaken well on into the autumn is enough to show that it had no real importance.
: i. e. round about 37-9.

. We know little of her beyond what is told us here, but her gentilicium suggests that she was probably related to Vespasian by blood, and her cognomen that she was connected with one of the Domitiae gentes. It seems clear that the coins and inscriptions which mention diva Domitilla are to be referred to Vespasian's daughter rather than to his wife, for Statius (Silv. 1. 1. 97), in speaking of the crowd of deified relations who will welcome Domitian to heaven, ibit in amplexus natus fraterque paterque et soror, makes no mention of his mother. Probably therefore the Domitilla Augusta of the inscriptions is also the daughter. On this basis Mommsen (Droit public, v, p. 99, note 4) assigns, of inscriptions, to Vespasian's wife only the titulus found at Herculaneum (CIL. x. 1419 = Dessau 257), where neither title is present. She died before 69.
. Nothing more is known of Statilius Capella.
. Sabrata (Sabart), in the neighbourhood of the Lesser Syrtis, was a town of Phoenician origin and one of the three civitates of Tripolis: later a Roman colony. ...

. Any one accused of being a slave who wished to vindicate his free status could have his case adjudicated by reciperatores: his spokesman was called assertor. We learn from this passage that a similar process could be adopted for vindicating contested Roman citizenship. Probably it is owing to a misunderstanding of Suetonius' language that (pseudo) Aurelius Victor in two places (Epit. 10. 1, 11. 1) refers to Domitilla as a freedwoman; this we are not told, though it is clear enough that Vespasian married beneath him. See for Latina condicio, Plin. Ep. 10. 5, and Hardy, ad loc.

. Vespasian's father-in-law, of whom we know nothing more. His position as quaestor's clerk was that purchased by Horace after the battle of Philippi, and was a more honourable one than Suetonius implies: many scribae quaestorii were, or became, of equestrian rank.
. Ferentium or Ferentis was a small municipium in south Etruria, just off the Via Cassia, the ancestral home of the emperor Otho (Suet. Oth. 1).

. Titus (Flavius Vespasianus) was born prope Septizonium ' in a little dark room of a mean house' (Suet. Tit. 1), his father being obviously in some degree of poverty at the time. The date of his birth was 30th December (ib.) of the year 39: Suetonius indeed says 41-insigni anno Gaiana nece-but since Dio (66. 18) gives his age on coming to the throne (23rd or 24th June 79) as 39 years 5 months 25 days-a figure which takes us back to 30th December 39, and is moreover confirmed by Suetonius himself (Tit. 11) when he speaks of Titus as dying (13th September 81) in his forty-second year we can only conclude that Suetonius is correct in his day of the year but made a mistake in the year itself.

. Domitian (T. Flavius Domitianus) was born in a house called ad Malum Punicum, afterwards consecrated as a temple of the Gens Flavia, on 24th October 51 (Suet. Dom. 1); he was thus nearly twelve years younger than Titus. He received his cognomen from his mother Domitilla (see note on c. 2 ad init.).

. Flavia Domitilla: she was probably older than Domitian; if not, she must have died at latest when barely seventeen, having already married and borne a child. But even so the honours she received, consecration and the nomen Augustae (see above), were doubtless due to her imperial blood rather than to any intrinsic importance. Her husband's name is unknown; the fact that their daughter was a Flavia does not necessarily mean that he was a Flavius, for adoption into the imperial family might well account for it. This daughter was the Flavia Domitilla (the third of that name) who married Flavius Clemens-two sons of this marriage were regarded by Domitian as his successors (Suet. Dom. 15), and was later exiled, almost certainly as a Christian (on this point see e. g. Meyer, Ursprung und Anfänge des Christentums, iii, p. 553 sq.). The following table shows the family of Vespasian: Sabinus ? Flavius Sabinus Flavius Liberalis Vespasian Flavia Domitilla Titus Flavia Domitilla ? Domitian Flavius Clemens Flavia Domitilla Vespasianus Domitianus five others (CİL. vi. 8942 = Dessau 1839).

. Antonia Caenis (CIL. vi. 12037). If Vespasian made a bad match he had made a good liaison, for Caenis was already a trusted confidential servant of Antonia's in 31 (Dio 66. 14), and possibly Vespasian's advancement was in part due to her influence. She must have been nearly fifty when Vespasian's wife died, but he remained faithful to his former love for her until her death, and treated her 'almost as a lawful wife', a state of things of which Domitian (and no doubt other orthodox Romans) strongly disapproved (Suet. Dom. 12).

. This was the lady known as Antonia minor (36 в. с. -A.D. 37), daughter of M. Antonius the triumvir, wife of the elder Drusus, and mother of Germanicus and Claudius. She is little heard of in the disputes of the other Julio-Claudian widows, but exerted none the less considerable political influence. She numbered among her personal friends and dependents distinguished Jews and Orientals, and client princes, besides Roman senators of the highest rank.

div.p: §1. Narcissi. This is the famous freedman of Claudius, his secretary ab epistulis, who exercised immense influence in Rome during the first half of the reign. It has even been suggested that the conquest of Britain was directly inspired by him, though all we know for certain is that when the legions arrived at Boulogne, and objected mutinously to being shipped across the Channel, it was he that was sent to pacify them (Dio 60. 19). Doubtless it was through his influence also that Titus was introduced to court as the familiaris of Britannicus; his name at any rate is mentioned in connexion with the two boys (Suet. Tit. 2). What were his reasons for favouring Vespasian, or what return Vespasian made him, is unknown.

p.note: . He was legate of the II Augusta (Tac. Hist. 3. 44), a legion stationed in Upper Germany at Argentoratum (Strassburg) before it was detailed to form part of the army of invasion. It remained in Britain until the end of the Roman occupation. The praefectus castrorum of this legion under Vespasian in Britain was a certain P. Anicius Maximus (CIL. iii. 6809 = Dessau 2696).

. The then governor of Upper Germany was the future emperor Galba. There is little record of Vespasian's activities in this command: the two estimates we possess, both exaggerating by implication his military position (ἄνδρα... προειρηνεύσαντα μὲν πάλαι ῾Ρωμαίοις τὴν ἑσπέραν ὑπὸ Γερμανῶν ταρασσομένην, Jos. B. I. 3. 1. 2; compescet ripis Rhenum, Sil. Ital. 3. 599), do not suggest any considerable campaigns. It has been supposed that the words of Eutropius (7. 19), in Germaniam et deinde in Britanniam missus tricies et bis cum hoste conflixerit, as contrasted with the tricies (in Britannia) of Suetonius, refer to two victories in Germany, but it seems most improbable that this divergence is anything but a mistake in the MSS. of one or the other author.

. For a succinct account of the Claudian invasion of Britain in 43 see Anderson's ed. of Tac. Agricola, Introduction, p. xlvi sq. Vespasian distinguished himself at the first battle, the crossing of a difficult river (Medway?) (Dio 60. 20); he was present also at the capture of Camulodunum, under the auspices of Claudius himself (see below). From this base three bodies of invasion proceeded to further conquest: the II legion under Vespasian formed the left wing, and overran south England -a tile found at Honey-ditches (near Seaton in Devonshire) records a temporary camp of the II legion there (Eph. Epigr. ix. 12688). In 47 Vespasian was still in Britain, according to Dio's chronology (60. 30: Dio, however, tells in this connexion an impossible story of Titus (eight years old!) saving his father's life); he presumably returned to Rome later in the year with A. Plautius.

: these are usually identified as the Belgae (Hampshire and Wiltshire) and the Atrebates (Berkshire). See e. g. Teuber, Beiträge zur Geschichte der Eroberung Britanniens durch die Römer, p. 52. insulam Vectem = the Isle of Wight: Suetonius' description,
, is vague, but more accurate at least than Pliny's, inter Hiberniam ac Britanniam (Ν. Η. 4. 103).

. A. Plautius had been consul suffectus in 29, and governor of a province for two or three years up to 43 (CIL. v. 698 = Dessau 5889): probably this was Pannonia; thence came the IX Hispana, one of the legions detailed for the invasion. Probably also he was related to the emperor's first wife, Plautia Urgulanilla. He received an ovation on his return in 47, an honour very rarely granted except to members of the imperial family. Claudi ipsius ductu. Claudius was anxious that a part of the credit for the conquest should be his, and under his instructions A. Plautius delayed the decisive battle at the crossing of the Thames until he could arrive. The emperor was therefore able to superintend in person the capture of Camulodunum (Colchester), the capital of the Trinovantes, and to return to Rome to celebrate his triumph having spent sixteen days only in Britain (Dio 60. 23).

div.p: § 2. triumphalia ornamenta. The triumph was by this time strictly a prerogative of the imperial house, but on the analogy of the consularia and similar ornamenta, a successful military commander could be given the triumphalia ornamenta, conferring on him the title and privileges of a man who had triumphed, without the triumph itself-Vespasian is thus quite properly described as senex triumphalis (Tac. Hist. 4. 8). Such an honour was decreed by the Senate, but usually on the emperor's proposal, a fact which was often recorded by the recipient (see e.g. inscription of Ti. Plautius Silvanus Aelianus-'auctore Vespasiano', CIL. xiv. 3608 = Dessau 986). Vespasian himself had doubtless well earned the distinction, but that Claudius was extravagantly lavish in granting it we learn both from Suetonius (Claud. 24) and from Tacitus (Ann. 11. 20).

p.note: . One of these was presumably the augurate, an office prominently displayed later on Vespasian's coins (Eckhel, vi, p. 331). For other examples of duplex and triplex sacerdotium see Dessau in J. R. S. 1913, p. 306.

. Vespasian was thus consul suffectus in November and December: since Domitian was born 'while his father was consul designatus, in the month preceding his entry to office' (Suet. Dom. 1), and was in his forty-fifth year at the time of his death (18th September 96) (ib. 17; Dio 67. 18), the year must have been 51, a year noteworthy in consular annals from the fact that Claudius (in spite of Suet. Claud. 14) was consul for nine if not for ten months (Bullet. dell' inst. 1871, p. 151). On the reduction in the term of the consulship under the empire see Mommsen, Droit public, iii, p. 93 sq.; other two-months' consulships occur in 37 (Suet. Claud. 7) and 54 (ib. 46).

. Narcissus began to lose his influence at court through the consequences of the very act that he had planned to strengthen it, namely, the downfall of Messalina in 48. For when Claudius came to select a new wife, Narcissus failed to gain that position for his candidate, Aelia Paetina, and thereafter Agrippina, the successful competitor, used every means in her power to bring him into disfavour. On the death of Claudius in 54, which, even so, was plotted in Narcissus' absence, he was one of the first victims of the new reign. Agrippina's period of ascendancy over her son was short, two years at most, but presumably Vespasian's withdrawal from public life would last until her murder in 59 left him free from personal enemies at court.

div.p: § 3. sortitus Africam. The governors of Africa, unless for some special reason, were chosen by lot from among the consulares of sufficiently long standing (see Tac. Agric. 42). The interval at this time between the consulship and the African command was from eight to thirteen years (Mommsen, Droit public, iii, p. 288), so that Vespasian's year can hardly have come before 59-60, and this agrees with the period of his secessus through fear of Agrippina (see above). On the other hand he must have held the command before his second secessus in 65 or 66 (see below), and probably a year or two before, to judge by the events recorded by Suetonius in between. We may probably therefore date his governorship to one of the five years from 60 to 64 (see Pallu de Lessert, Fastes des provinces africaines, i, p. 139 sq.).

p.note: . This estimate is not altogether borne out by Tacitus' description-proconsulatum ... famosum invisumque egerat (Hist. 2. 97; cf. the attitude of Africa and her army on his accession, ib. 4. 49), nor by Suetonius' own account of the turnip-riot at Hadrumetum, nor by his use of the word certe, 'at any rate', implying that there might be a difference of opinion about what preceded; only Silius Italicu Italicus, for what his evidence is worth, concurs-reget impiger Afros (3. 599). On the other hand Tacitus agrees that Vespasian was in some financial straits on his return from Africa (see below). We may conclude therefore (1) that his administration was not corrupt, (2) that it was very unpopular-no doubt he displayed, in Africa also, those qualities, parsimony and insistence on military discipline, that met with so much unfavourable criticism later.
: Hadrumetum (Sousse), a city of Phoenician origin on the coast of the old province, the site of Caesar's landing in 47. ...

. Cf. the poverty and squalor of Domitian's early youth, i. e. about this time (Suet. Dom. I). That Vespasian was forced to mortgage his estates to his brother Sabinus is recorded also by Tacitus, who adds that this unbrotherly method of financial aid was believed to have caused ill-feeling between the two, making Sabinus unwilling to associate himself actively with Vespasian's imperial aspirations (Hist. 3. 65).

. The word mango signified a dealer who by means of artifices assigned a spurious value to his goods, most often slaves or live-stock, whose value would fluctuate according to their condition: Vespasian's nickname implies that his dealings were in mules. Trading of this kind was of course regarded as dishonourable to a senator, but no doubt it was profitable: we hear of gorgeously-apparelled trains of mules being supplied at this time for the service of Nero and Poppaea (Suet. Ner. 30; Dio. 62. 28); possibly some of these actually came through Vespasian.

div.p: § 4. Peregrinatione Achaica: i.e. Nero's tour in Greece in 66. This episode in Vespasian's life is complicated by the diversity of our authorities. Tacitus tells us, in connexion with Nero's stageperformances at Rome at the quinquennial games of 65, ferebant Vespasianum, tamquam somno coniveret, a Phoebo liberto increpitum aegreque meliorum precibus obtectum, mox imminentem perniciem maiore fato effugisse (Ann. 16. 5), and it has been assumed that this and the account in Suetonius are two versions of the same episode, (1) because Vespasian's caution would have kept him from offending twice in the same way, (2) because this freedman Phoebus reappears as the insolent usher in the story of Dio (66. 11), ἐπὶ τοῦ Νέρωνος ἐσκυθρωπακότα ποτὲ αὐτὸν (Vespasian) ἐπὶ τοῦ θεάτρου ἐν τῇ Ἑλλάδι (this story occurs also, though without the usher's name, in Suet. Vesp. 14). Did the two accounts really refer to the same episode, Suetonius' version would surely be correct, for if Vespasian were virtually exiled in 65, he could not have accompanied Nero to Greece in 66, and that he did go to Greece is plainly state stated by Dio, Suetonius (in c. 5 also), and Josephus (B. I. 3. 1. 3). But the supposed identity seems to me improbable: Tacitus' account rather suggests than excludes another lapse later; that Vespasian could not have given offence twice is not in accordance with Suetonius' saepius; nor is it very extraordinary that the same freedman who was spying on senators in Rome should have the duty of denying them audience in Greece. I conclude, therefore, that Vespasian offended first in Rome, when he was saved by the intercession of of his friends, offended again in Greece, and was punished by banishment from court.

p.note: . Similarly Thrasea Paetus had been forbidden to pay the usual congratulatory call at the birth of Nero's daughter in 63, a prohibition which was regarded as a praenuntia imminentis caedis (Tac. Ann. 15. 23).

. This second secessus was of short duration, two or three months at most. For Nero did not leave for Greece until 25th September 66 (Henzen, Acta Arv., p. lxxxiv), and Vespasian must have been appointed to the Jewish command very early in 67 at latest. Since he sailed from Greece to Judaea (Jos. B. I. 3. 1. 3), the civitas in question was probably there or thereabouts.

div.p: § 5. vetus et constans opinio. Josephus gives the oracle as follows: κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν ἐκεῖνον ἀπὸ τῆς χώρας αὐτῶν τις ἄρξει τῆς οἰκουμένης (Β. I. 6. 5. 4); on it see W. Weber, Josephus und Vespasian, p. 35 sq.; as he points out, Josephus is doubtless correct in citing the prophecy as of a single conqueror : Tacitus less accurately refers it, profecti Iudaea, to Vespasian and Titus (Hist. 5. 13), but Suetonius, with rather characteristic slovenliness, Iudaea profecti, to Vespasian alone.

p.note: : so Josephus thought (loc. cit.), but the Jews as a body accepted neither the imperial nor the Christian realization of their prophecy (for the latter see Eusebius, Hist. Eccles. 3. 8); e. g. one of the leaders of their revolt under Hadrian was a Simon Bar-Kocheba (i. e. son of a star; cf. Numbers xxiv. 17), a title indicating his assumption of the rôle of Messiah. caeso praeposito. This was Gessius Florus, appointed to the procuratorship of Judaea in 64 or 65, apparently on the strength of having married an intimate friend of Poppaea's (Jos. A. I. 20. II. 1). Suetonius seems to have made a mistake here: it is difficult, if not impossible, to understand by caeso anything except 'killed', and Florus was not killed; he retired to Caesarea (Jos. B. I. 2. 15.6).

. Cestius Gallus, appointed in 63 (if the correction of the MSS. in Tac. Ann. 15.25 is correct). For the story of his campaign in Judaea see Josephus (B. I. 2. 19). He died soon after, fato aut taedio, while still in office (Tac. Hist. 5. 10).

. If an eagle was lost it must have been that of the XII Fulminata, which alone was present in force (Jos. B. I. 2. 18. 9). But Josephus' account, though recording that the XII legion was held to be dishonoured (ib. 7. 1. 3), does not mention this crowning disgrace: the story therefore is improbable (so Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa, xii. 1706).
. Nero was quite right: Vespasian would never have rebelled against him.

div.p: § 6. additis... duabus legionibus. For the Jewish War Vespasian was given three legions-V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XV Apollinaris; what exactly Suetonius means by 'two legions were added to the forces' is uncertain. If it means 'to the forces in Judaea', Suetonius is in error, for there was no legion there. It cannot refer to two legions being brought from Alexandria by Titus (Jos. B. I. 3. 1. 3), for the text of Josephus has been shown to be faulty here, and it is clear that only one was brought the MSS. read τὸν μὲν υἱὸν Τίτον ἔστειλεν (Vespasian) ἐπ᾿ ᾿Αλεξανδρείας, τό τε πέμπτον καὶ τὸ δέκατον ἐκεῖθεν ἀναστήσοντα τάγμα, but this is inconsistent with ζεύγνυσι (Titus) τὸ ἀχθὲν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ πεντεκαιδέκατον later on (3. 4. 2), and the alteration to τὸ πέμπτον καὶ δέκατον is easy (so Niese, and see Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa, xii. 1574). It might mean that Vespasian was given, in addition to one Syrian legion (X), two non- Syrian legions (V and XV), which should have returned to their respective stations on the conclusion of Corbulo's Armenian war, but were detained in the East on account of the condition of Judaea (see Mommsen, Roman Provinces, Eng. trans., ii, p. 211 n.) On the whole, however, it seems most likely that Suetonius wrongly imagined one legion already in Judaea; for that there were alae and cohortes there is confirmed by Josephus (B. I. 3. 4. 2), though he gives different figures. (See below.)

p.note: , cohortibus decem. Josephus (loc. cit.) gives five alae and eighteen cohortes, added to the one ala and five cohortes already in Judaea. No doubt his figures are correct.

. Titus was made legate of a legion (legioni praepositus, Suet. Tit. 4); this was clearly the XV Apollinaris, which he had been sent to bring from Alexandria (see above). Vespasian's other legati legionum were Sex. Vettulenus Cerialis, of the V Macedonica (Jos. B. I. 3. 7. 32), and the elder Trajan, of the X Fretensis (ib. 3. 7. 31).
: one of his notable conquests was the III Gallica legion (see on c. 6).
. Exactly in the same way Corbulo had to discipline the Syrian legions before he could trust them on military campaigns (Tac. Ann. 13. 35).
: at the siege of Jotapata in 67 (Jos. B. I. 3. 7. 22). Josephus makes him wounded by an arrow in the flat of the foot: doubtless his version is correct.

div.p: Suetonius gives no account of Vespasian's activities between the siege of Jotapata and his salutation as emperor (about two years). In the course of two campaigns in 67 and 68 he occupied and subdued the whole of Judaea except cept the city of Jerusalem (Tac. Hist. 5. 10). As he was about to proceed to this final task, he heard of the death of Nero, an event which automatically put an end to his appointment (Jos. B. I. 4. 9. 2): he waited therefore for further news. The news that came was of the accession of Galba, and Titus was sent to pay homage to him, it was rumoured with the hope that he would be adopted by the childless old emperor (Tac. Hist. 2. 1): a contradictory rumour asserted that Galba had sent assassins to murder Vespasian (Suet. Galb. 23). Anyway, when Titus reached Corinth he heard of Galba's assassination, and decided to return to Judaea, where both the Judaean and the Syrian armies had already taken the oath of allegiance to Otho (Tac. Hist. 2. 1-6; Suet. Tit. 5). Finally, when the news of the first battle of Bedriacum and of the death of Otho reached the East, they likewise took the oath of allegiance to Vitellius, unwillingly, Vespasian being not yet ready to declare himself (Tac. Hist. 2. 74).

§ 1. in spem...conceptam. The difference between 'entering into' a hope, and 'conceiving' it, is not very clear: Suetonius must mean that Vespasian had for long entertained the hope, but only now attempted the task of realizing it. The world at large thought nothing of his prospects until after the event (Tac. Hist. 1. 10).

p.note: . Suetonius describes eleven ostenta : (A) the branches of the oak-tree, (B) Vespasian's adventure as aedile, (C) the stray dog, (D) the ox, (E) the cypress tree, (F) Nero's tooth, (G) the oracle at Carmel, (H) the prophecy of Josephus, (I) Nero's dream, (J) the strange behaviour of Caesar's statue, (K) the three eagles at Bedriacum. Of these only the first and last are found in Suetonius alone. Tacitus gives (E) (G) (J) (Hist. 1. 86; 2. 78); Dio (B) (C) (D) (E) (F) (H) (I) (last six in 66. 1, (B) in 59. 12); Orosius (H) (7.9); Josephus (H) (naturally at greater length, B. I. 3. 8. 9); and Plutarch (J) (Oth. 4). These authors, moreover, record no other ostenta than these.

div.p: § 2. In suburbano... filius suus. On the various personages concerned in this oracle see on cc. I and 2. The theory of this oracle, like that of the cypress tree, was that the life of a family or individual could be bound up in the life of a tree, the Life-Tree (see Frazer, Balder the Beautiful, ii, p. 168).
§ 3. aedilem: see on c. 2.
§ 4. manum humanam : for the hand is the natural symbol of power: manus indeed is frequently used in this sense, especially in relation to the power of a husband over his wife (Gai. Inst. 1. 108).

p.note: . Dio (66. 1) says the tree was torn up ὑπὸ σφοδροῦ πνεύματος, Tacitus merely repente (Hist. 2.78). But clearly the point of the oracle was not in the tree's fall but in its resurgence. This episode occurred in Vespasian's youth (Tac. loc. cit.), so that the ager avitus must be his grandmother Tertulla's estate at Cosa. The sudden downfall of this same tree later heralded the murder of Domitian and the extinction of the Flavian dynasty (Suet. Dom. 15).

div.p: § 5. in atrium: i. e. from Nero's bedroom into the hall, where his courtiers would be respectfully waiting.

§ 6. Carmeli dei oraculum. Mt. Carmel is a spur of the Anti- Libanus, on the borders of Phoenicia, and stands up sheer from the 3236 Mediterranean. Probably there was not a proper oracle here, but there would be a place for sacrifice, and divination from entrails would be rendered more sure by the sanctity of the high place (see Bouché-Leclercq, Divination dans l'Antiquité, iii, p. 399). Orosius (7. 9) makes this the occasion of the Iudaea profecti oracle, but clearly he is wrong, for that was found ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς γράμμασιν (Jos. B. I. 6. 5. 4); what Vespasian was given was a personal fortune (Tac. Hist. 2. 78). Tacitus gives the priest's name, Basilides (to distinguished from the Basilides implicated in another imperial be portent; see on c. 7). pries

p.note: . This is the famous Jewish historian and antiquarian: the proper form of his name, Iosepus, is preserved in the Italian Giuseppe, but long usage in Latin has confounded it with the form Joseph (see Niese, Josephus, i, p. v). He was born in 37 or 38 (A. I. 20. 12), connected on his mother's side with the royal house of Judaea (Vita, I). He conducted the defence of Jotapata in 67, and when the town was captured fell into the hands of Vespasian; this was the occasion of his prophecy. On Vespasian's accession he was set free; he accompanied Titus to Rome in 71, was given the Roman citizenship by the emperor (hence his Roman gentilicium Flavius), and a grant of lands in Judaea. The date of his death is unknown (after 93). (See two recent works: Laqueur, Der jüdische Historiker Flavius Josephus; W. Weber, Josephus und Vespasian.) That Suetonius had no knowledge of the Bellum Iudaicum seems clear from the four discrepancies es in in his short account of the war: viz. with regard to the fate of Florus, the capture of the XII Fulminata eagle, the composition of Vespasian's forces, and the nature and cause of Vespasian's wound (see on c. 4). For Josephus' own account of this prophecy see B. I. 3. 8. 9. Dio (66. 1) makes Josephus say μετ᾿ ἐνιαυτὸν δὲ λύσεις αὐτοκράτωρ γενόμενος, which would make the prophet a little too sanguine.

div.p: § 7. tensam. The tensa was the sacred chariot that bore the attributes of the various gods in the solemn procession at the Circensian games. The dream thus implied that Vespasian was under the especial favour of Jupiter.

p.note: : i. e. at the end of 68. Galba was consul II ordinarius in 69 with T. Vinius. Tacitus (Hist. 1. 86) and Plutarch (Oth. 4) both put this prodigy in the reign of Otho.

: the decisive battle between the armies of Otho and Vitellius: its site is now identified with that of the modern village Calvatone, at the convergence of the Verona-Cremona and Hostilia-Cremona roads. Of the name Suetonius always uses the form Betriacum (also Oth. 9; Vit. 10 and 15: so Plutarch), Tacitus Bedriacum (so Josephus); Juvenal (2. 106) refers to Bebriacum.

div.p: § 1. nec tamen fortuito favore. This story, that the Moesian army at Aquileia was the first to acclaim Vespasian emperor, and that his subsequent actions were influenced by their support, is peculiar to Suetonius; in Tacitus the Moesian army (in Moesia) have plainly heard of Vespasian's salutation in the East before they move (Hist. 2. 85; so also Jos. B. 1. 4. 10. 6): Tacitus only says that the movements of Vespasian were hastened by the ardour of the Danube legions on his behalf. But there seems no reason to doubt Suetonius; his story reads like a temporary outburst of disaffection against Vitellius, soon placated (tunc quidem compressa res est) and may well have come from his father Suetonius Laetus, a tribune at this time in the Pannonian XIII Gemina legion (Suet. Oth. 10).

§ 2. Moesiaci exercitus. The three legions of the Moesian army were the III Gallica, VII Claudia, VIII Augusta. It is clear that Suetonius imagined them as sending detachments only in support of Otho; Tacitus' account is not so clear, and at first sight would seem to assume that these legions marched out en bloc-he talks about the Moesian legions arriving at Aquileia (Hist. 2. 46), and it is the legions that tear down the Vitellian vexilla there (ib. 2. 85). Yet these legions in his narrative are certainly back in Moesia in July or August, when they declared for Vespasian, and there is no mention of their return in the detailed account of the disposal of the Othonian forces (ib. 2. 66-7). As therefore Suetonius' narrative probably rests here also on the information of his father (see above), and as it is not certain what Tacitus means to imply, it is perhaps safer to assume that he means by legiones 'legionary forces' (as he certainly does in Hist. 2. 30), and that detachments only were sent to Italy (see Filow, Die Legionen der Provinz Moesia, p. 24, and Hardy in J. of Ph., 1910, p. 136). ...

p.note: . On this point Tacitus differs definitely; he makes the arrival of the forces from Moesia at Aquileia announced to Otho immediately after the battle (Hist. 2.46). It is impossible to decide whose chronology is correct.
. Aquileia was in Venetia, at the north-east corner of Italy, the natural point of concentration for troops from the Danube provinces. It was about 125 miles as the crow flies from Bedriacum.
: cf. Tac. Hist. 2. 85.

div.p: § 3. e legione tertia. The III Gallica legion, transferred from Syria to Moesia in 67-68 (see Filow, op. cit., p. 11, and Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa, xii. 1521). It had had a long and distinguished career in the East (Tac. Hist. 3. 24), whence it brought a custom that helped to decide the coming battle (ib.). Tacitus agrees that it favoured Vespasian- tertiam legionem, quod e Syria in Moesiam transisset, suam numerabat (ib. 2. 74, where suam clearly refers to Vespasian, not to Mucianus), as also that it was the instigator in Flavian support (ib. 2.85). Its legate was at this time T. Aurelius Fulvus, grandfather of the emperor Antoninus Pius (ib. 1. 79; CIL. iii. 6741 = Dessau 232).

p.note: . Ti. Iulius Alexander was the son of a Jew named Alexander, alabarch (i. e. head of the Arab customhouse officials) at Alexandria (Jos. A. I. 20. 5. 2), and the nephew of the Jewish philosopher Philo (ib. 18. 8. 1), but was himself an apostate (Tacitus thus calls him an Egyptian, Hist. I. 11). He was procurator of Judaea from about 45 to 48 (Jos. A. I. 20. 5. 2), served in Corbulo's Armenian war in 63 (inlustris eques Romanus, Tac. Ann. 15. 28), and was made praefectus of Egypt in 66 (Jos. B. 1. 2. 15. 1): : his two legions were the III Cyrenaica and the XXII Deiotariana. Tacitus' narrative refers also to his favour for Vespasian (Hist. 2. 74): one interesting link between the two is furnished by the fact that Alexander the alabarch was one of the many Jews in the entourage of Antonia (Jos. A. 1. 19. 5. 1; see on c. 3). Tacitus and Dio (66.8) also ascribe the first salutation to the Egyptian legions: Josephus gives the credit to Judaea (B. I. 4. 10. 4-6). Ti. Alexander served afterwards as chief of staff to Titus and was present at the capture of Jerusalem. On his famous edict as praefectus of Egypt (IGR. i. 1263, OGI. 669, partly given in Bruns, Fontes, p. 243 sq.) see Stuart Jones, Fresh Light on Roman Bureaucracy, p. 35 sq.

. Tacitus also says of this day, Ist July 69, isque primus principatus dies in posterum celebratus (Hist. 2. 79). Vespasian reckoned the years of his tribunicia potestas from this date, though it was not till 22nd December that the Lex conferring it was promulgated by the Senate (see note on c. 12).

.: i. e. 11th July. Tacitus (loc. cit.) says V. Nonas Jul., i. e. 3rd July. The difference may well be only a MSS. error in one of the two authors, for it is clear that Suetonius and Tacitus are using the same source here (cf. similarity of phrase quoted above and apud ipsum iuravit = Tacitus' apud ipsum iurasset). The only advantage of Suetonius' date is that this would give time for the news of the proclamation at Alexandria to have reached Judaea. Josephus (B. I. 4. 9. 9) records that Vespasian started for an expedition from Caesarea on 23rd June (πέμπτῃ Δαισίου μηνός), but this too must be an error (Dessau, Gesch. der römischen Kaiserzeit, ii. 1, p. 351).

div.p: § 4. ultionem mandantis. This means it was written after Otho had been defeated and before he committed suicide, a period in which he certainly wrote other letters (Suet. Oth. 10).

p.note: . The same story is in Tacitus (Hist. 2. 80), who adds that the rumour was set afoot by Mucianus.

: C. Licinius Mucianus (CIL. xiv. 2173), the chief instrument of Vespasian's accession, appointed governor of Syria with the command over four legions in 67 in succession to Cestius Gallus; Nero no doubt selected him, like Vespasian, as a capable administrator and an improbable rebel. He had been virtually exiled by Claudius, and his reputation in private life was bad; even after Nero's death it is clear that in spite of his great influence and authority he was not regarded as a possible emperor : Tacitus' epigram on him is well-known-cui expeditius fuerit tradere imperium quam obtinere (Hist. I. 10). That Mucianus and Vespasian had previously been at enmity, while governors of adjacent provinces, is also recorded by Tacitus (ib. 2. 5); his story is that it was Mucianus' friendship with Titus that finally led him to support Vespasian, and to urge him to make a bid for empire (ib. 2. 74-7. This story is criticized by Kappelmacher). On Vespasian's salutation by the legions, Mucianus was dispatched with troops for the attack on Italy, but only arrived when the decisive battle had been fought and Vitellius was dead. In spite of this, he at once assumed the position of Vespasian's regent and almost of his colleague, a position which he was loath to lay down on Vespasian's return (see c. 13). He died apparently after 75 (dramatic date of Tacitus' Dialogus, in which he is spoken of as though living, c. 37); before 77 (date of publication of Pliny's Natural History, in which he is spoken of as though dead). Pliny in this work refers constantly to his writings, which were voluminous, dealing chiefly with his personal investigations in the realms of geography, natural history, and art-criticism. (See for an account of him Kappelmacher in Pauly-Wissowa, xiii. 436 sq.)

. Vologaesus (there are various spellings of the name) was the famous Parthian monarch who in the reig reign of Nero had warred against Corbulo: his dates of rule are from 51 to about 78. Tacitus (Hist. 4. 51) puts this offer, or rather the receipt of this offer, after the news of Cremona had reached the East (40,000 equites he says, but of course in the Parthian army these were the same as sagittarii); but the distances were great, and probably Vologaesus was a bona fide supporter, and his offer may well have been made as a reply to the envoys previously sent by Vespasian (ib. 2. 82). Tacitus adds that Vespasian declined the offer, urging that ambassadors should be sent to the Senate (an act of constitutional etiquette on his part).

div.p: § 1. Suscepto civili bello. The Civil War was of course set on foot by Vespasian allowing himself to be saluted imperator, not by any movements of troops.

p.note: . The troops sent from the eastern provinces consisted of a body of light-armed soldiers under Mucianus, followed by the VI Ferrata legion in force and detachments from the other legions numbering 13,000 men (Tac. Hist. 2.83). But no doubt Suetonius is referring also to the troops of the Danube army, which indeed had decided the issue long before Mucianus arrived. ...

. So Tacitus in the same phrase exactly-Vespasianum obtinere claustra Aegypti placuit (Hist. 2. 82). This phrase was apparently a standard one for describing the peculiar strategic position of Egypt-it does not mean 'the two strongholds of Egypt' (Alexandria and Pelusium), but rather the stronghold of Egypt' (i. e. Aegypti is a genitive of definition). Cf. the passage in the Annals (2. 59) where we are told that the importance of Egypt consisted in (1) the opportunity it afforded its possessor of reducing Rome to subjection by cutting off her corn supply, (2) its power of defence even by a small force against a large army. Cf. also Josephus (B. I. 4. 10. 5), where these reasons precisely are ascribed to Vespasian in occupying it. This was of course why Augustus refused to allow senators to enter Egypt without permission, and gave the command of the province to an eques who was practically his viceroy (see Hardy, Monumentum Ancyranum, p. 125).

. The Serapeum at Alexandria was a noted oracle (see the excursus on Serapis in Tac. Hist. 4. 83-4: Serapidis dei, quem dedita superstitionibus gens ante alios colit (ib. 4. 81), and Bouché-Leclercq, Divination dans l'Antiquité, iii, p. 377 sq.).

. Many editors have proposed here to alter libertus into liberius or uberius, so as to get rid of the divergence of Suetonius from Tacitus (Hist. 4. 82), who makes Basilides an Egyptian noble. But there is much variation in the two accounts even apart from this, for Tacitus dates Vespasian's visit to the Serapeum after his remedial miracles, and puts both episodes, not in his period of uncertainty, but while he is assuredly emperor and only waiting for favourable winds to return to Rome. The point of the oracle is left obscure by Suetonius: it lay in Basilides' namevim responsi ex nomine Basilidis interpretatus est (Tac. loc. cit.).

. Clearly Suetonius has made a mistake here: the news of the victory at Cremona (the second battle of Bedriacum) and of Vitellius' death would not reach Vespasian simultaneously, as there was about two months between the two events (27th October-21st December). According to Tacitus (Hist. 3. 48) Vespasian had not yet reached Alexandria when the news of Cremona was brought him, so that if Suetonius' dating of this story be correct (see above), it must have been the death of Vitellius that these letters announced. It may be noted 1 that Suetonius gives in this Life no account of the decisive battle, nor of Vitellius' last days, doubtless because Vespasian himself was not present.

div.p: § 2. e plebe quidam ..nec eventus defuit. This story is also told by Tacitus (Hist. 4. 81) and by Dio (66. 8), with the difference that an infirmity of the hand is substituted in the second case for one of the leg. Tacitus adds that even when he wrote there were eye-witnesses to testify to the event, even postquam nullum mendacio pretium. (See G. G. Ramsay's notes on this passage of Tacitus, p. 389 of his translation.)

§ 1. in urbem reversus. There is a record in the Acts of the Arval Brothers (Henzen, p. xcvii) of an immolation to Fortuna Redux on the occasion of the emperor's return to Rome: unfortunately there is no indication of the date. We know, however, the following facts: (1) Vespasian was still in Alexandria at the time of an extraordinarily high Nile flood (Dio 66. 8)-the Nile does not reach its maximum till about 20th July. (2) He had left Alexandria for Rome before the final capture of Jerusalem (2nd September) could be announced in Egypt (Dio-Zon. 66. 9). (3) Titus received at Berytus the news of his father's safe arrival after he had celebrated his father's birthday, i. e. after 17th November (Jos. B. I. 7. 3. 1; 7.4.1): we may conclude therefore that Vespasian left Egypt some time in August 70 and reached Rome some time late in September or early in October. The reason for this long delay is not obvious, for Tacitus tells us that Vespasian was only waiting for the summer winds (Hist. 4. 81), and, moreover, that his anxiety to return was heightened by the news of the profligate behaviour of Domitian (Hist. 4. 51); perhaps his original plan was to wait until he and Titus could return together, but increasing impatience decided him to depart alone (so Dio-Zon. 66. 9).

p.note: . Titus had brought the Jewish war to an end by the capture of the upper city of Jerusalem (2nd September 70), but he remained in the East during the whole of the winter, and it was not until the middle of June 71 that he was back in Rome (Chambalu in Philologus, xliv, p. 507 sq.: the tribunicia potestas of Titus dates from Ist July 71). Vespasian and Titus then triumphed in common (though the Senate had decreed a separate triumph to each), a few days only after Titus' return (Jos. B. 1. 7. 5. 3), and while Domitian was still consul, i. e. before the end of June (συνέπεμπε δέ σφισιν αὐτὰ καὶ ὁ Δομετιανὸς ὑπατεύων ἐπὶ κέλητος, Dio-Zon. 66. 12). The details of the triumphal procession and the accompanying spoils from Jerusalem are given by Josephus (B. I. 7. 5. 3-7). Many coins also were struck celebrating the victory, e.g. Mattingly, Numismatic Chronicle, 1921, p. 200, with the legend Iudaea devicta and a representation of Judaea in an attitude of defeat, but the conquest was not considered glorious enough enough for either father or son to take the cognomen 'Iudaicus' (Dio 66. 7).

. Vespasian was consul ordinarius in every year of his principate but two-he had already assumed the consulship for 70 at Alexandria (Tac. Hist. 4. 38), so that Suetonius' expression is not strictly accurate. Clearly this large number of consulships (a return to the first system of Augustus, 27-23 B. C.) was part of his dynastic policy: he was anxious to lose no opportunity of adding lustre to the Flavian name, and the constant association of Titus in his father's honours (Titus was Vespasian's colleague in all the consulships but one, 71) was another step to assure the succession. At the same time and as part of the same policy the number of consules suffecti was increased, and their term of office reduced (on the consular Fasti for Vespasian's reign see Asbach, Bonner Jahrb. 1885, pp. 105-77; and cf. Anderson's Agricola, p. 168). The full record of Vespasian's imperial consulships is as follows: II. 70 January 1, with Titus I: Still consul April 1 (CIL. vi. 126, if interpretation is correct): proprobably for four months. bably Mucianus II and Petillius III. 71 January 1, with M. Cocceius Nerva: probably for two months. IV. 72 January 1, with Titus II : for four months. V. 74 January 1, with Titus III: for twelve days. VI. 75 January 1, with Titus IV : length of tenure known. un- Cerialis were consuls May and June, if record of June 25,... NL ... (Fasti Fer. Lat.) can be made to read LL..., and see Jos. B. I. 7. 4. 2. Domitian I consul April 5 with Cn. Pedius Cascus (CIL. x. 867 = Dessau 1990), May (CIG. iii. 5838) and June 25 (Fasti Fer. Lat.) with C. Flavius Sabinus II consuls May 29 (ib.). Titus and Ti. Plautius Silvanus Aelianus II consuls January 13 (CIL. i. 774 = Dessau 5161. i). But seems to have retired before Titus, if mutilated piece of Acta Arv. inscription (Henzen, p. xcix) refers to consuls, as CIL. vi. 32361 makes it do. In this case it was Titus who retired early. But L. Iunius Caesennius Paetus and P. Calvisius Ruso consuls March 1 (CIL. vi. 597 = Dessau 3534: 79 most probable year-see Dessau in J. R. S. 1913, p. 305), and Domitian had another consulship (VI) before them.

. Vespasian assumed the censorship with Titus as his colleague: he saw in it a most valuable instrument for the reorganization of the State, and had decided on making use of it from the beginning of his reign-Titus is already described as censor designatus in an inscription of the second half of 71, immediately after his return from the East (Dessau 258). The censorship began early in 73-Vespasian is first described as censor after he has been designated for his fifth consulship, before his fifth tribunicia potestas, i. e. between about the end of March and Ist July 73 (CIL. vi. 1238)-; it ended (officially) in 74 after the normal eighteen months-Censorinus dates the lustral sacrifice to this year (de Die Natali, 18. 14)-, but certain events of the year 75, such as the enlargement of the pomerium (CIL. vi. 1232 = Dessau 248: this however had been authorized in the Lex de Imperio), are probably to be connected with this office. Vespasian is called (retrospectively) censor in inscriptions until the end of his reign. The inscriptions dealing with the censorship are conveniently collected in H. C. Newton, The Epigraphical Evidence for the Reigns of Vespasian and Titus, p. 28 sq. ...

. Suetonius gives us here one of his rare flashes of historical insight and power of expression. It would be hard to define Vespasian's policy more clearly or more succinctly than in this sentence, on which the rest of the Life is really nothing more than a commentary. ...

div.p: § 2. Milites inter se agebant. Suetonius now proposes to discuss the actions of Vespasian in regard to the army and the provinces; he gives first the general reasons why these two departments of the empire demanded attention. In both cases the reasons given seem superficial: Vespasian's great military rearrangements were caused, not by the Civil War, but by the German rebellion and the mutiny of the Rhine army, which Suetonius does not even mention; and the changes in status of the client kingdoms and free cities of the East were largely due (1) to the reorganization of the eastern frontier, (2) to the need for increasing taxation in the empire: only as regards Achaia and possibly Lycia is there reason to suppose that internal dissensions were the cause of the change.

p.note: . This statement is misleading, and indeed inaccurate as it stands. The four Vitellian legions whose eagles were present at the second battle of Bedriacum were the I Italica, V Alaudae, XXI Rapax, XXII Primigenia, and none of these were disbanded. Measures were certainly taken-by Mucianus before Vespasian's arrival-to reduce the number of the Praetorian cohorts (raised by Vitellius to sixteen, Tac. Hist. 2. 93), and at the same time make room for those Praetorians expelled by Vitellius who had espoused Vespasian's cause (ib. 2. 67): it was therefore proposed, by means of grants of land, to get rid of the Praetorians newly enrolled by Vitellius (ib. 4. 46). Even so Mucianus found himself faced with an impending mutiny, and quite unable to disband these men en masse: it had to be done gradually (carptim ac singuli, ib.: confirmed by inscriptions relating to three soldiers of Vitellian legions transferred into Praetorian cohorts, who received honesta missio after 8 years', 15 years', 3 years' service respectively, CIL. vi. 2725, 2649, 2558 = Dessau 2034-6). The number of cohorts was, however, reduced: only nine-the normal number-remain in the diploma of 2nd December 76 (CIL. iii, p. 853 = Dessau 1993). But it seems probable that Suetonius is referring also to the legions disbanded on the Rhine, and if so he has missed the point altogether, for they were disbanded not as Vitellians, but as mutineers. This is clear inter alia from the fact that the four legions disbanded, I, IV Macedonica, XV Primigenia, XVI, were the four whose eagles had remained in Germany (XV Primigenia did not mutiny, but surrendered at Castra Vetera).
