. Demands for donatives by the soldiers were an important factor in the Civil Wars (see index to G. G. Ramsay's translation of the Histories s. v. donative), and it was the opinion of Tacitus that Galba could have won over the Praetorians, quantulacumque parci senis liberalitate (Hist. 1. 18); Vespasian's stand against indiscriminate largesse was thus courageous. What Suetonius means by sero is not quite clear : Mucianus certainly gave the Flavian soldiery 25 denarii a head as soon as he reached Rome (Dio 65. 22. This is 100 sesterces a head, and is very small in comparison with the 5,000 that Otho gave the Praetorians, Tac. Hist. 1. 82); but perhaps Suetonius is referring to a later payment made by Vespasian in person. The phrase etiam legitima praemia may be taken as identical with the parallel phrase in Tacitus about the moderation of Vespasian's promises, ne Vespasianus quidem plus civili bello obtulit quam alii in pace (Hist. 2. 82), i. e. a sum no larger than they would have obtained for ordinary military services.

div.p: § 3. ac ne quam occasionem • revocavit. Vespasian had always been known as a disciplinarian. Cf. his action at the beginning g of the Jewish War (c. 4), and the laudatory estimate of Tacitus, prorsus, si avaritia abesset, antiquis ducibus par (Hist. 2. 5), no doubt referring partly to this side of his character. suppose the point of Vespasian's remark was, that he would rather have a boorish manly praefectus than a cultured effeminate one (to smell of garlic being the mark of the yokel). I

p.note: . Apparently this 'shoe-money' was a recognized form of indirect donative: cf. Tac. Hist. 3. 50, of Antonius' army on the march to Rome, seditiosae militum voces... clavarium (donativi nomen est) flagitantium : clavarium = 'shoenail money'. Vespasian's order was thus a sort of grim practical joke: he would do away with this particular excuse in future. Hirschfeld thinks that these men were couriers (Kaiserliche Verwaltungsbeamten 2, p. 228).

div.p: § 4. Achaiam. Nero had granted libertas to the whole province of Achaia at the end of his visit there in 66-7, i.e. he had rendered it immune from Roman tribute and outside the jurisdiction - of any Roman official. Vespasian abruptly cancelled this grant, declaring ἀπομεμαθηκέναι τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τὸ ῾Ελληνικόν, 'that the Greeks had forgotten how to be free' (Paus. 7. 17). Against the resentment of the Greek population of the empire (e. g. the philosopher Apollonius, Philostr. Apoll. 5. 41), he pleaded acute internal dissensions (which even Philostratus admits existed, though οὔπω τῆς ἐπὶ τοσόνδ᾽ ὀργῆς, loc. cit.), but doubtless he had principally in mind the needs of the imperial exchequer. (It must be noted, however, that liberae civitates did not always possess immunitassee instances in Tac. Ann. 12. 61-3). Achaia became a senatorial province under a proconsul of praetorian rank; at the same time it seems to have been reduced in size by the inclusion of Thessaly in the province of Macedonia and the isolation of Acarnania and the Epirus under a procurator. The date of the change is not certain. Philostratus (loc. cit.) puts it in 70, during Vespasian's visit to Achaia on his voyage back to Rome: if so, it is strange that Josephus does not mention it, though he refers to the visit (B. I. 7. 2. 1). A more probable date is that given in the Chronicle of Eusebius, year of Abraham 2090 = Ist October 73-30th September 74. Now all these alterations in the status of free cities and kingdoms, it is true, are cited together in the Chronicle under this year, and in some cases, where we have other evidence, the year is unsatisfactory; but Eusebius must have had some reason for his dating, and most probably this was that the change in the status of Achaia was ascertained to have fallen in this year; the other changes were then merely appended as they followed in Suetonius.

p.note: . Claudius had taken away the libertas of the Lycians ob exitiabiles inter se discordias (Suet. Claud. 25); it must then have been restored by Nero (after 57, Tac. Ann. 13. 33). Vespasian now formed the imperial province of Lycia and Pamphylia (Pamphylia formerly went with Galatia, Tac. Hist. 2. 9): we know of two legati during his reign, Sex. Marcius Priscus and L. Luscius Ocrea (IGR. iii. 609, 466). The date is uncertain (73-4 Chron. Euseb., but see above).

. The libertas of the Rhodians, adempta saepe aut firmata (Tac. Ann. 12. 58), had first been taken away by Claudius (Dio 60. 24), then restored by him in 53, when the young Nero pleaded their cause (Suet. Claud. 25; Ner. 7; Tac. loc. cit.). Rhodes would now be included in the province of Asia. There is a strange passage in Festus (Brev. 10) to the effect that under Vespasian a provincia Insularum was established: certainly no such independent administrative province existed until the reforms of Diocletian, but McElderry suggests (J. R. S. 1913, p. 119 sq.) that there may have been a financial procuratorship of the islands established now similar to the provincia Hellesponti recorded about this time (inscription of C. Minicius Italus, CIL. v. 875 = Dessau 1374), and thus Festus may have 'preserved by accident a fragment of genuine history'. As to the date of the Rhodian loss of libertas we only know that Rhodes was free at the time of the 'Ροδιακός of Dio Chrysostom, an oration usually assigned to the beginning of Vespasian's reign. Possibly the change was one of the reforms in the province of Asia due to the prolonged governorship of T. Clodius Eprius Marcellus (70-3; see McElderry, loc. cit.). It is noteworthy that Vespasian called at Rhodes and Lycia, as well as Achaia, on his voyage from Alexandria to Rome in 70 (Jos. B. I. 7. 2. 1; Dio-Zon. 66.9); he had thus some first-hand knowledge of conditions in free states. But probably his main reason for the change was financial (cf. our designs on the ἀτέλεια of the Channel Islands).

. Another state whose libertas was frequently taken away and restored (see Mommsen, Roman Provinces, Eng. trans., i, p. 306). It formed part of the province of Pontus and Bithynia (Plin. Ep. 10. 43): the date of the change in its status seems to have been after 77, for Pliny's Natural History, published in that year, speaks of Byzantium as liberae condicionis (4. 46). Pontus and Bithynia apparently became an imperial province for a short time about 78 (Hirschfeld, Kaiserliche Verwaltungsbeamten², p. 374: this is contested however by Rostovtzeff, Ann. of B. S. A., xxii, p. 15 sq.), and possibly we may assign the incorporation of Byzantium to this period.
. Doubtless incorporated at the same time and under the same conditions as Rhodes, but we have no further evidence about it.

. This celebrated emendation of the Thraciam Ciliciam of the MSS. was first proposed by Turnebus. The MSS. reading is obviously wrong: Thrace and Cilicia proper had both long been governed directly from Rome (Thrace, e. g. Tac. Hist. 1. 11; Cilicia, e. g. ib. Ann. 13. 33). On the other hand we know from Dio (59.8) that Gaius on his accession handed over to Antiochus IV Commagene, καὶ προσέτι καὶ τὰ παραθαλάσσια τῆς Κιλικίας, and although he afterwards rescinded the grant, Claudius restored it (Dio 60. 8), with Cilicia Maritima still an adjunct to the kingdom (Tac. Ann. 12. 55). Since this part of Cilicia was commonly called aspera or τραχεῖα on account of its infertility, it seems quite certain that this is what Suetonius is referring to, and that the reading of the MSS. must be altered accordingly. Cilicia Maritima will then have been incorporated in the empire at the same time as Commagene (see below).

. The story of the deposition of the king of Commagene (still Antiochus IV) is given in Josephus (B. 1. 1.7.7 7. 7. 1-3) and is dated to the year 72 (ἔτος τέταρτον Οὐεσπασιανοῦ διέποντος τὴν ἡγεμονίαν, reckoning by the years of the calendar), before July, when Josephus' narrative ends. Although his forces had taken part in the Armenian War of Corbulo (Tac. Ann. 13. 7) and in the Jewish War (ib. Hist. 5. 1; Jos. B. I. 5. 11. 3), and he had, moreover, supported Vespasian's candidature for empire (Tac. Hist. 2. 81), yet he was now accused by Caesennius Paetus, governor of Syria, of planning an alliance with Parthia. This was serious news, for at Samosata on the Euphrates the Parthian empire impinged on Commagene, and such an alliance would mean a direct route open for a Parthian invasion of Syria. Paetus was therefore given instructions to act as he thought best, which he obeyed by taking the X legion, marching into Commagene, and deposing Antiochus. Antiochus himself submitted without resistance, but his sons Epiphanes and Callinicus first offered battle (cf. bellum Commagenicum in CIL. iii. 143871 = Dessau 9198), and then fled to Parthia, where they were surrendered to a centurion C. Velius Rufus, sent to retrieve them (Dessau 9200). All three were generously treated by Vespasian; Epiphanes' son Philopappus was adlected into the Senate by Trajan and attained the consulship (CIL. iii. 552 = Dessau 845). It is said that the emperor Gaius learnt from Antiochus the arts of tyranny (Dio 59.24): this means that Antiochus was probably one of Antonia's coterie (see on c. 3), and would thus be well known to Vespasian in his earlier life. Commagene was incorporated in the province of Syria; its capital was henceforth known as Samosata Flavia.

p.mentioned: dicionis regiae usque ad id tempus
p.note: . This is not strictly accurate; after the death of Antiochus III Commagene had been made in 18 a province of praetorian rank (Tac. Ann. 2. 56), and it was only Claudius who finally reconstituted the kingdom (see on Trachiam Ciliciam above). The Antiochi were a Seleucid dynasty, descended from Laodice, daughter of Antiochus VIII Grypus (see tables in Bouché-Leclercq, Histoire des Séleucides, ii, p. 647).

. pro equite Romano. Cappadocia had been made a province by Tiberius in 18 (Tac. Ann. 2. 56), and assigned to imperial procurators of equestrian rank (Dio 57. 17, e. g. Iulius Paelignus in 51, Tac. Ann. 12. 49). Vespasian now turned it into a first-class province, with a governor of consular rank and two legions. Both the consularis rector and the legiones have been questioned, the presumption being that Suetonius was here thinking of the conditions in his own time. We may note at the outset that the two statements stand or fall together, i. e. a consular governor implies more than one legion and vice versa. But in both cases there are independent reasons for believing in Suetonius' accuracy. (1) With regard to the legions, it is pointed out that only the XII Fulminata is mentioned as having been sent to Cappadocia at this time (Jos. B. I. 7. 1. 3), and that the second legion stationed there under Hadrian, the XV Apollinaris, was under Vespasian in Pannonia (ib. 7. 5. 3, and inscriptions). Suetonius' legiones, however, is corroborated by Tacitus (Hist. 2. 81), and there is one legion, the newly-created XVI Flavia, whose station under Vespasian is unknown. Probably therefore it and the XII formed the garrison of Cappadocia during his reign (so Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa, xii. 1765). (2) Ti. Iulius Celsus Polemaeanus, a senator of praetorian rank, is described in an inscription from Ephesus (Dessau 8971) as leg. Aug. divorum Vespasiani et Titi provinciae Cappadociae et Galatiae, Ponti, Pisidiae, Paphlagoniae, Armeniae Minoris. We know, however, of two consular governors in Vespasian's reign, Cn. Pompeius Collega (CIL. iii. 306 (inaccurate) Dessau 8904) and M. Hirrius Fronto Neratius Pansa (IGR. iii. 223), and the clue to Polemaeanus' position is provided by the fact that Fronto's governorship also continued under Titus, as many coins attest; i. e. he and Polemaeanus were in the province at the same time. Polemaeanus therefore was his subordinate, and probably analogous to the iuridici in the Western Provinces (see on him Cumont, Acad. Belg. Bull. cl. d. lettr., 1905, p. 197 sq., Ritterling, Oest. Jahresh., 1907, p. 299 sq., and Groag in Pauly-Wissowa, x. 544 sq.). = The XII legion was sent to Melitene in Cappadocia in the autumn of 70; the formation of the province was then presumably one of the first acts of Vespasian's reign, though the first mention of it in inscriptions is in January-July 76. As reorganized it came to include much more than Cappadocia alone (see inscription of Polemaeanus quoted above, and Cumont in Anatolian Studies presented to Sir William Ramsay, p. 109 sq.). The reasons for the change are not very lucidly given in Suetonius' propter adsiduos

. The point was that since Rome had abandoned under Nero the system of maintaining her own nominee on the throne of Armenia, and had allowed it to be occupied by a Parthian prince (though a vassal of Rome), a legionary force in Cappadocia was essential. See for a discussion of the eastern frontier problem Henderson's Nero, p. 153 sq. he seems wrong, however, in thinking that the Neronian arrangements brought about complete peace with Parthia until the reign of Trajan. There were certainly hostilities in 76-7, for the elder Trajan, governor of Syria at that time, was awarded the triumphalia insignia for successes in a Parthian war (Plin. Paneg. 14 and 16). The statement of Aurelius Victor, bello rex Parthorum Vologesus in pacem coactus (Caes. 9. 11), is probably only a misreading of the reference to Vologaesus in c. 6 of this Life.

div.p: § 5. Deformis urbs. Suetonius gives a selection only of Vespasian's building operations. For a list of many more see Weynand in Pauly-Wissowa, vi. 2689.

p.note: . The Capitoline temple had been completely destroyed, on 19th December 69, by the Vitellian army in its attack on Sabinus (Tac. Hist. 3. 71). Dio too records (66. 10) that Vespasian, immediately on his return to Rome in 70, started with his own hand the rebuilding of the temple. A religious ceremony, the consecration of the ground and the foundation-stone laying, had already taken place on 21st June in Vespasian's absence (Tac. Hist. 4. 53). Some writers still suppose that Suetonius and Dio are referring to this event, but all the evidence is against them : Vespasian certa certainly did not reach Rome till months after 21st June (see above), nor would the praetor Helvidius Priscus have officiated if Vespasian had been present; and in any case, the ceremony described by Tacitus was clearly inaugural only. An eques, L. Iulius Vestinus, was appointed to superintend the restoration (Tac. loc. cit.): Vestinus, though a distinguished man, was a native of Gallia Narbonensis (or. Claudii Lugdunensis = Dessau 212), and no doubt this appointment gave great offence to the Senate. The temple, six-columned, was apparently finished in 71 (see the coins of Vespasian's third consulship in Cohen, Vespasien, nos. 486 sq.). It was again destroyed by fire immediately after Vespasian's death (Plut. Poplicola 15).

. This reads like a more detailed account of the commission recorded by Tacitus (Hist. 4. 40), qui aera legum vetustate delapsa noscerent figerentque. On this see Jordan, Topographie der Stadt Rom, i. 2, p. 55.

div.p: § 1. templum Pacis. Begun by Vespasian immediately after his triumph in 71 (Jos. B. I. 7. 5. 7), to celebrate the return of peace to the empire and the closing of the temple of Janus (this last only in Oros. 7. 9, quoting however-7. 3, 7. 19-a lost book of the Histories, fr. 4 and 5 of the Oxford text). It was dedicated at the beginning of 75 (Dio 66. 15). Vespasian used the ground, southeast of the Forum of Augustus, which had been left free by the fire in 64: works of art and sculptures from every land were placed in the temple, among others the golden vessels taken by Titus from Jerusalem.

p.note: . This temple existed until the time of Constantine: it stood on the Caelian Hill and occupied part of the site of the Golden House of Nero: Claudia diffusas ubi porticus explicat umbras, ultima pars aulae deficientis erat. (Mart. Spect. 2.) On it see Jordan, Topographie der Stadt Rom, i. 3, p. 232 sq. On Nero's neglect of his predecessor's 's honours see (pseudo) Seneca, Octavia 249 and Suet. Claud. 45-in numerum deorum relatus (Claudius); quem honorem a Nerone destitutum abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum. Claudius, however, is called Divus in inscriptions throughout Nero's reign, though strangely enough not in the Lex de imperio Vespasiani: possibly it was the participation of Claudius in the sodales Augustales (there is, as a matter of fact, no mention of sodales Augustales Claudiales before the reign of Trajan) that originated under Vespasian in connexion with the new temple.

. This was the famous Amphitheatrum Flavium, known as the Colosseum since the Middle Ages. It was built on the site of the lake of Nero's Golden House, in the hollow between the Esquiline and the Caelian Hills: hic ubi conspicui venerabilis Amphitheatri erigitur moles, stagna Neronis erant. (Mart. loc. cit.) It was built three stages high by Vespasian, two were added by Titus, and it was finally completed by Domitian (Chronogr. a. 354, p. 146, ed. Mommsen). 3236

div.p: § 2. recenso senatu et equite. This, of course, was one of the acts of Vespasian's censorship: on the whole subject of the composition of the Senate at this time see B. Stech, Senatores Romani qui fuerint inde a Vespasiano usque ad Traiani exitum. As censor also V Vespasian created new patricians (for the lists and evidence see Stech, op. cit., p. 133: to which add P. Calvisius Ruso, inscr. in J. R. S. 1913, p. 302).

p.note: . Among those expelled from the Senate was M. Palfurius Sura (Suet. Dom. 13; schol. Juv. 4. 53).

. adlecto. Adlectio in senatum was the means employed by the emperor for the advancement of capable persons, worthy of seats in the Senate and of the higher magistracies and governorships, but unwilling, or too old, to go through the customary routine of minor offices. Such men would be adlected inter praetorios, inter aedilicios or tribunicios (these were alternative stages), or inter quaestorios, and would have the position and privileges of one who had been praetor, aedile, tribune, or quaestor, in the regular way. Vespasian's adlectiones in 73-4 during his censorship with Titus were of course quite constitutional, taking place in connexion with the lectio senatus of which Suetonius speaks. Of the following list nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 certainly, and others probably, were adlected during this period. On the other hand no. 16 certainly, and nos. II and 14 possibly, were adlected in 69, immediately after Vespasian's salutation by the eastern legions, when plerosque senatorii ordinis honore percoluit, egregios viros et mox summa adeptos (Tac. Hist. 2.82). This action of Vespasian's was clearly a usurpation of power: it seems, however, to have established a precedent, for future emperors assumed the censoria potestas as a part of the imperial powers, Domitian with the title censor perpetuus, Trajan and his successors without even the authority that such a title could give them. As regards the individuals adlected by Vespasian, there are three examples (nos. 1, 2, and 3) of men of the ordo senatorius raised to higher rank by this means: most of those recorded, however, are Italians and provincials of non-senatorial family, as Suetonius rightly says (cf. Tac. Ann. 3. 55). Of these many, nos. 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, and 14, are known to have previously been distinguished members of the equestrian service. The object of Vespasian's policy of adlectio was clearly to make a path for such experienced administrators into the higher service of the State, but it had the effect also of giving the emperors as complete a control over the personnel as they had previously had over the activities of the Senate. The following examples of adlecti in senatum by Vespasian are known: A. Inter praetorios. I. C. Iulius Cornutus Tertullus, cos. suff. 100 with Pliny. CIL. xiv. 2925 = Dessau 1024. Already, however, a senator of aedile rank. 2. Cn. Domitius Curvius Tullus. CIL. xi. 5211 = Dessau 991. Already a tribunicius and praetor designatus when sent to Africa as legatus; apsens inter praetorios relatus. Possibly this promotion was not technically adlectio, but since the dates indicate that it fell within the period of Vespasian and Titus' censorship, it perhaps deserves to be included. 3. L. Antistius Rusticus. Inscr. in J. R. S. 1924, p. 180. A laticlavius. 4. Q. Aurelius Pactumeius Fronto, from Cirta in Numidia, cos. suff. 80. CIL. viii. 7058 = Dessau 1001, and Année épig. 1914, no. 247. Described as the first consul from Africa. 5. Q. Aurelius Pactumeius Clemens, from Cirta in Numidia. CIL. viii. 7057. 6. C. Salvius Liberalis Nonius Bassus, on whom see on c. 13 CIL. ix. 5533 = Dessau 1011. Adlected first inter tribunicios, later inter praetorios. 7. C. Caristanius Fronto, from Antioch in Pisidia. Inscr. in J. R. S. 1913, p. 260 = Dessau 9485. An eques, prefect of an ala of Bosporani. Adlected first inter tribunicios, then promotus inter praetorios. No emperor's name, but obviously by Vespasian. 8. C. Fulvius Lupus Servilianus, from Nîmes. CIL. xii. 3166. An eques, prefect of the ala Longiniana. 9.... tilius Lo...us. CIL. iii. 335. An eques, prefect of the III cohort of sagittarii. 10. L. Baebius Avitus. CIL. vi. 1359 = Dessau 1378. An eques, procurator of Lusitania. [He is described merely as adlectus inter praetorios, without emperor's name: Gsell therefore suggested (L'Empereur Domitien, p. 72) that he was adlected by Domitian; but the inscription was apparently cut during Vespasian's lifetime.] Possibly also II. C. Antius A. Iulius Quadratus, from Pergamum, cos. suff. 93, cos. 11 ord. 105. Numerous inscriptions relate to him, but none mention any offices held before he became legatus pro praetore of Pontus and Bithynia; it seems therefore plausible to suppose that he was adlected inter praetorios by Vespasian (see Waddington, Fastes des provinces asiatiques, no. 114, p. 172 sq.). If so, he was one of those adlected privately in 69, for he was already an Arval Brother in 72 (Henzen, p. xcvi). 12. Baebius Massa, the famous delator. Procurator of Africa in 70 (Tac. Hist. 4. 50), proconsul of Baetica before 93 (ib. Agric. 45): clearly therefore he was adlected by one of the Flavian emperors, and this would no doubt be inter praetorios, as he was a distinguished eques. Mention may also be made of 13. Minicius Macrinus, described by Pliny as equestris ordinis princeps, quia nihil altius voluit: adlectus enim a divo Vespasiano inter praetorios honestam quietem huic nostrae ambitioni dicam an dignitati constantissime praetulit (Ep. 1. 14), i. e. he was adlected, but refused the honour. B. Inter aedilicios. 14. Ti. Julius Celsus Polemaeanus, from Ephesus, cos. suff. 92. Dessau 8971; see Cumont, Acad. Belg. Bull. cl. d. lettr. 1905, p. 197 sq.; Ritterling, Oest. Jahresh. 1907, p. 299 sq.; Groag in Pauly-Wissowa, x. 544 sq. An eques, tribune of the III Cyrenaica legion. Since the inscription merely says adlecto inter aedilicios ab divo Vespasiano, with no mention of Titus nor of the censorial function, it seems plausible to assume that he was one of those adlected privately by Vespasian in 69: this would be a reward for services rendered as tribune of a legion then stationed at Alexandria. C. Inter tribunicios. 15. C. Salvius Liberalis Nonius Bassus = no. 6. C. Caristanius Fronto = no. 7. (name unknown), from Tarragona. CIL. ii. 4130. D. In gradum incertum. 16. L. Plotius Grypus, cos. suff. 88. By private action of Vespasian in 69 (Tac. Hist. 3. 52). Praetor in 70 (ib. 4. 39): adlected therefore inter aedilicios or inter tribunicios. 17. L. Antonius Saturninus, the rebel of 89. ᾿Αντώνιος Σατορνίνος ἐνεγράφη. Aelian fr. 112. παρὰ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ ἐς τὴν βουλὴν It may be noted that Rutilius Gallicus (Q. Iulius Cordinus C. Rutilius Gallicus) was previously thought to have been adlected by Vespasian on the grounds that the sketch of his career given by Statius (Silv. 1. 4) suggests that he was originally in the equestrian service, and does not allude to any senatorial office held by him before the praetorship. But the inscription found at Ephesus in 1913 (Dessau 9499) now shows clearly that he went through the whole of the senatorial cursus, As regards the equestrian order, there is much less evidence for its personnel at this time. We know of two men made equites by Vespasian,--Hormus, one of his freedmen (Tac. Hist. 3. 12; 4.39), and Claudius, the imperial secretary a rationibus (Stat. (Stat. Silv. 3. 3. 143). But these are bad examples; they rather typify the sort of men, powerful dependents, that previous emperors would have equestrianized, than the honestissimi whom Vespasian desired to introduce.

. Vespasian meant that the two orders differed in rank rather than in privilege. This was one of the grievances of the senators: what the senatorial order had lost in prestige under the empire the equestrian order had gained, and it was beginning to be found that the position of eques, as compared with the position of senator, was more lucrative, more important in its duties, more secure under emperors like Nero or Domitian, and only to a small extent less honourable. Thus we find men preferring an equestrian to a senatorial career; the sentiments of Minicius Macrinus have been quoted above (no. 13 of the adlecti in senatum): cf. those of Annaeus Mela (Tac. Ann. 16. 17) and Cornelius Fuscus (ib. Hist. 2.86). The policy of adlectio was conceived partly no doubt to make the senatorial service more agreeable; cf. also the shortening in the term of the consulships, designed partly to give more senators the chance of attaining this supreme honour.

div.p: This pressure of cases before the civil courts was one of the natural results of the wars of 69: the prolonged cessation of justice caused by them had resulted in the postponement and accumulation of normal cases, and the volume of these was swelled by the abnormal disputes as to ownership of property inevitable after the successive confiscations and grants of rival commanders. Vespasian's commissioners were appointed (1) to adjudicate these ownership-ofproperty disputes, (2) to review the list of cases up before the centumviri and to deal themselves with those which appeared unnecessary or easy of settlement. Since the courts of the centumviri provided now the chief opportunity for ambitious advocates to display their talents, their business was often unduly protracted by forensic eloquence; Pliny shows himself an avowed supporter of their lengthy and leisurely procedure (Ep. 1. 20; 6. 2).

p.note: . This regulation formed part of the law called by the lawyers the SC Claudianum, and was really only a revival of a measure carried through the Senate by Claudius in 52, of which Pallas was the repertor: it contained a proviso that if the slave's master had consented to the marriage, the woman should remain free (Tac. Ann. 12. 53). See Buckland, Text-book of Roman Law, p. 71.

. This also revived or strengthened a measure of Claudius (the SC Macedonianum, so called apparently after a notorious usurer). The restrictions on such practices imposed by Claudius in 47 (Tac. Ann. 11. 13) are unknown, but clearly his intention was to restrain the saevitia of the moneylenders, Vespasian's rather to control the luxuria of the young men. See on its provisions Buckland, op. cit., p. 462 sq.

: i.e. he behaved as a citizen among citizens, οὐχ ὡς αὐτοκράτωρ ἀλλ' ὡς ἰδιώτης, in Dio's phrase (66. 10). Augustus was of course the paragon of civilitas (Suet. Aug. 51 sq.), and this was the chief virtue that the Roman public demanded in its emperor; the principle seemed to be that as long as the emperor behaved like an ordinary citizen, the people were content to believe that he was nothing more. One can, however, detect a certain difference between the Augustan and the Flavian virtue: Augustus' behaviour is clearly dictated by his whole constitutional policy, while Vespasian's attitude seems rather that of the affable and benevolent autocrat, too good-natured to be haughty, and conscious, moreover, that regal display would contrast ludicrously with his former plebeian position (μνήμῃ τῆς προτέρας αὐτοῦ τύχης, Dio loc. cit.); that he could act despotically is shown by his treatment of the Alexandrians (ib. 66. 8). ... ad conditores Herculis. For legends of the connexion between Hercules and Reate cf. Varro, de lingua Latina 5. 53.
: i.e. the triumph over the Jews in 71: see note on c. 8.

... There is clearly an hiatus after these words in the text, but the meaning of the passage must be that Vespasian did not assume the tribunicia potestas at once; the obvious way therefore to fill the gap is to suppose that statim has fallen out after pote-statem. What exactly Suetonius means is doubtful: the tribunicia potestas must have been conferred on Vespasian as a consequence of the Senatusconsultum of 22nd December 69 (for the date see Weynand in Pauly- Wissowa, vi. 2640-1) with all his other imperial privileges (senatus cuncta principibus solita Vespasiano decernit, Tac. Hist. 4. 3, cf. decernitur Othoni tribunicia potestas et nomen Augusti et omnes principum honores, ib. I. 47), and it occurs among his titles on the diploma of 7th March 70 (CIL. iii, p. 849 = Dessau 1989). Mommsen (Droit public, v, p. 151) explains the phrase as a reference to the interval between the Senatusconsultum which arranged that the Lex should be drawn up and the comitia tribuniciae potestatis which passed the Lex, -i. e. the still partially extant Lex de Imperio, an interval that varied in length from 12 to 53 days; on this interpretation Suetonius would merely mean that Vespasian was content to wait rather longer than some emperors for the comitia (we have no record when these were held). It seems strange, however, that if Suetonius meant all this he did not say so, and perhaps we need only suppose that he had forgotten either (1) that it was the Senate which initiated the conferring of the tribunicia potestas, or (2) that the Senate was controlled by Vitellius for the first months of Vespasian's imperium, and so assumed that Vespasian himself chose not to receive the tribunicia potestas until December. That Suetonius always thought of Vespasian's reign as beginning on Ist July is shown by his very next sentence, where he records an imperial act as happening

. The years of Vespasian's tribunicia potestas are reckoned from this date, i. e. he is trib. pot. II on Ist July 70, and so on. This arrangement of Vespasian's, dating his reign from his salutation by the troops, is another example of his indifference to forms: we may contrast the dies imperii of the similarly-situated Vitellius, fixed at 19th April, the date on which he was recognized by the Senate (Henzen, p. xciv).

. It was not customary for emperors to assume this title immediately (Appian, B. C. 2.7; see Mommsen, Droit public, v, p. 40). Vespasian does not bear the title on the diploma of 7th March 70 (CIL. iii, p. 849 = Dessau 1989), but a coin of Ephesus (Cohen, Vespasien, p. 373) gives him it while still in the first year of his tribunicia potestas, i. e. before Ist July 70.
. So Dio (60. 3; 66. 10). It was Claudius, quamquam iactator civilitatis, who instituted this practice (Suet. Claud. 35).

. Cf. for Vespasian's toleration of παρρησία Dio 66. 11. It may be observed that Suetonius first summarizes, as so often, the purport of the chapter, then gives one example each of the amicus, the causidicus, and the philosophus.

. On him see note on c. 6. His character and his relations with Titus are hinted at by Tacitus (Hist. I. 10; 2.5). The meaning of Vespasian's remark is obvious; it is noteworthy that he was the only one of Suetonius' twelve Caesars (except Claudius) who would have been entitled to make it.

. C. Salvius Liberalis Nonius Bassus, four times quinquennalis at Urbs Salvia in Picenum, was adlected into the Senate, first inter tribunicios, later inter praetorios, by Vespasian and Titus during their censorship (CIL. ix. 5533 = Dessau IOII). He had a distinguished senatorial career, being probably iuridicus of Britain under Vespasian and Titus, consul suffectus and proconsul of Macedonia under Domitian. Later in Domitian's reign he was accused of maiestas (Plin. Ep. 3. 9), and apparently banished: his name does not appear in the Acts of the Arval Brothers, of whom he was one, between 87 and 101 (Henzen, cxix and cxxxix). Under Trajan he was certainly again in Rome, but we find him refusing the proconsulate of Asia (which had been allotted to him), probably on account of his old age (tit. cit.). His eloquence as a lawyer is twice alluded to by Pliny (Ep. 2. 11; 3. 9).

. This may possibly be Ti. Claudius Hipparchus, the grandfather of Ti. Claudius Atticus Herodes the Athenian millionaire, of whom Philostratus says (Soph. 2. 1): ὁ μὲν γὰρ πάππος αὐτοῦ Ἱππαρχος ἐδημεύθη τὴν οὐσίαν ἐπὶ τυραννικαῖς αἰτίαις, ἃς ᾿Αθηναῖοι μὲν οὐκ ἐπῆγον, ὁ δ᾽ αὐτοκράτωρ οὐκ ἠγνόησεν. An inscription (CIA. iii. 38) mentions τὰ Ἱππάρχου χωρία τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ φίσκου πραθέντα. The dates fit, and the explanation of this retort, that Hipparchus' wealth ought not to be a reason for his accusation or condemnation, fits with Philostratus' story also. But the identification is of course only a conjecture.

. The most famous of the Cynic philosophers of the time: Seneca was his friend and admirer, and Paetus Thrasea chose to converse with him in his last hours. In 70 he defended the delator P. Egnatius Celer, a proceeding which Tacitus stigmatizes as disgraceful (Hist. 4. 40). Soon after 71, according to the chronology of Dio, a general expulsion of philosophers from Italy on the grounds of captious opposition was decided upon at the instigation of Mucianus: two, Hostilianus and Demetrius, suffered relegatio in insulam. See Dio (66. 13), who makes Vespasian send a message to Demetrius : σὺ μὲν πάντα ποιεῖς ἵνα σε ἀποκτείνω, ἐγὼ δὲ κύνα ὑλακτοῦντα οὐ φονεύω.

. Suetonius (Vit. 6) mentions only one daughter of the emperor Vitellius, by his second wife Galeria Fundana; her image appears with those of her father and brother on coins (see Mattingly, Coins of the Roman Empire in the British Museum, vol. i, e. g. Plate 61, no. 4). She was married early in 69 to Valerius Asiaticus, governor of Gallia Belgica, and consul designatus at the beginning of 70 (Tac. Hist. 1. 59; 4.4). This man then had presumably died, a conclusion which supports his identification with the D. Valerius (?) Asiaticus of CIL. vi. 1528, who died while consul designatus. Splendidissime probably means that the husband provided by Vespasian was a senator; at any rate (pseudo) Aurelius Victor understood it so (splendidissimo coniungeret viro, Epit. 9. 2). As to Vitellius' other relations, his young son Germanicus was put to death by Mucianus (Tac. Hist. 4. 80), but two adfines, L. Tampius Flavianus (ib. 3. 4) and C. Calpetanus Rantius Quirinalis Valerius Festus¹ (ib. 4. 49), both became consuls under Vespasian. Vespasian owed a debt of gratitude to Vitellius for some service rendered when L. Vitellius was censor (or consul) with Claudius (Vitellii cliens, cum Vitellius collega Claudio foret, Tac. Hist. 3. 66 it is not quite clear whether Vitellii means the father or the son); what service is referred to is unknown.
: i. e. fitted a house out. ...
. On the intricacies of this story see note on c. 4: Dio's version (66. 11) has been cited there. The usher was apparently a freedman named Phoebus.
is an invented word signifying 'the land of disease': ἐς κόρακας is Dio's equivalent, and 'the foule ill take thee' Philemon Holland's.

. This man is usually identified with the L. Pompusius Mettius of CIL. vi. 1495, praefectus of the aerarium Saturni from 77 to 80: the only difficulty about this identification is that these praefecti were commonly of praetorian rank, and our Mettius, as we see, was consul before the end of Vespasian's reign. I should prefer to suppose therefore that the two men were distinct, but that there was a close family connexion is obvious. Domitian was not so kind to Mettius' 'imperial horoscope': Mettius was first relegated to Corsica and afterwards killed by his orders (Suet. Dom. 10; Dio 67. 12), about the year 91.
. Dio reports Vespasian's words, πάντως μου μνημονεύσει καὶ πάντως με ἀντιτιμήσει (loc. cit.); meaning: if he does become emperor I shall have a claim to his gratitude.

: i. e. no innocent person was put to death during the reign, with the exception of those executed (1) in Vespasian's absence (no doubt referring to the acts of Mucianus in the early part of 70, Tac. Hist. 4. II; 4. 80), (2) without his knowledge (perhaps meaning the victims of Titus' zeal as praefectus praetorio, Suet. Tit. 6), or (3) at any rate against his 1 Surely this man's adfinitas would be through Valerius Asiaticus. will and by misleading him (this last reservation is rather obscure but probably refers to the story of the death of Helvidius Priscussee below, who would technically be regarded as insons).

. The celebrated Stoic, husband of Paetus Thrasea's daughter Fannia: he was a native of Cluviae (a Samnite municipium) and the son of a primipilaris (Tac. Hist. 4. 5). Whether he is the same as the legatus legionis in 51, tribune in 56 (ib. Ann. 12. 49; 13. 28) seems doubtful; if he is, we can hardly accept the statement of Probus (schol. Juv. 5. 36) that Helvidius was quaestor under Nero. In 66 he suffered relegatio following the process against his father-in-law (Tac. Ann. 16. 33); he was recalled by Galba (ib. Hist. 4. 6), and became praetor in 70, in which capacity he officiated at the foundation ceremony of the Capitoline temple on 21st June (ib. 4. 53). From the very beginning of Vespasian's reign we find him opposing official motions in the Senate: he objected to the congratulatory embassy to Vespasian being selected by lot, and proposed that it should be chosen by the magistrates on oath (Tac. Hist. 4. 6); he proposed that the question of curtailments in public expenditure should be left to the Senate, and not referred to the emperor (ib. 4.9); &c. All this opposition seems rather for the sake of opposition; Helvidius was anxious to find traces of the autocrat in what Vespasian did, and was disappointed when there were none to find. Nevertheless, he was, like Paetus Thrasea, a great hero in the eyes of Tacitus and Pliny: Dio, however (66. 12. Exc. Vat. 273), has some very sensible remarks to make about the distinction between the two. 'Helvidius was Thrasea's son-in-law and affected to emulate him, but in fact behaved very differently. For although Thrasea did not love Nero, in whose time he lived, yet neither did he treat him insolently by word or deed, save in so far as not thinking it proper to make himself a partner in what was done by him. But Helvidius hated Vespasian, and could not leave him alone in private or in public; thus by his deeds he was courting death.' Τὴν τοῦ Θρασέου παρρησίαν οὐ σὺν καιρῷ μιμούμενος is Xi is Xiphilinus' summary of this estimate. As to the date of Helvidius' death, we can only say that the chronology of Dio fixes it between 71 and 75. If we can believe Probus (loc. cit.), Helvidius had already been put on trial for his attacks on Vespasian but praeter spem absolutus est; he had also apparently been ejected from the Senate in 70 (στρατηγῶν τηνικαῦτα) for the same reason (Dio 66. 12. This account, however, parallels so exactly what had already happened to him under Vitellius-Tac. Hist. 2. 91 - that one is inclined to suspect it).
: i. e. there were no complimentary remarks or prayers for the emperor's welfare, such as were customary in documents issued by magistrates.
: i.e. 'degraded', used of magistrates whose authority was insulted (cf. Suet. Claud. 38). Apparently the metaphor was a military one.

. Pliny calls it exsilium (Fannia bis maritum secuta in exsilium est, Ep. 7. 19), but the previous banishment under Nero had certainly been relegatio (Tac. Ann. 16. 35), so that we may imagine Pliny to be speaking loosely (as also Tacitus, Hist. I. 3, secutae maritos in exsilia coniuges, obviously referring to Fannia). The distinction is that relegatio did not imply loss of civil rights, and was thus a more lenient form of banishment. Cf. Ovid's words (Trist. 5. 11. 21): pse relegati, non exsulis, utitur in me nomine.

. There is an hiatus in the MSS. which must be filled by some such words as laetatus est et. Ramsay supposes (The Church in the Roman Empire, p. 257) that Suetonius in the second half of the sentence is referring to the punishment of Christians (cf. the use of the word supplicia about them in Ner. 16): 'We have here indubitably a reference to some class of individuals, whose punishment Vespasian felt himself compelled to accept while he regretted it; for it is inconceivable that Vespasian, a Roman, a soldier of long experience in the bloody wars of Britain and Judaea, wept and groaned at every 'merited' execution.' This no doubt is true, but we are told by Dio (66. 12) in very similar words, συνεχύθη τε ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς καὶ δακρύσας ἐκ τοῦ βουλευτηρίου ἐξῆλθε, τοσοῦτον μόνον ὑπειπὼν ὅτι “ ἐμὲ μὲν υἱὸς διαδέξεται, ἢ οὐδεὶς ἄλλος.” In the text of Xiphilinus, as we have it, these words follow the story of the ejection of Helvidius Priscus from the Senate (see above), but an hiatus has long been suspected on account of the extreme inapplicability of Vespasian's remark to that occasion (Suetonius puts it post adsiduas in se coniurationes; see note on c. 25), and this suspicion the excerpt from Dio in Petrus Patricius (exc. Vat. 105) seems to confirm. Now if we may suppose, to make Dio's context for the remark agree with Suetonius', that some reference to a conspiracy and its punishment has dropped out of the text of Xiphilinus, it would appear reasonable to assume that the phrase of Suetonius before us rather refers to the same occasion, i. e. that it was conspirators, of however obvious guilt, that Vespasian punished reluctantly and with tears. (Cf. also for his weeping Dio 66. 16, in connexion with the execution of Iulius Sabinus, the Gallic rebel, and his wife.)

div.p: § 1. pecuniae cupiditas. Chapters 16 to 19 really read together, on this plan: 'Vespasian made every effort to raise money; some say he was naturally avaricious, but others reply that he was forced to be extortionate by the financial needs of the State, and cite his acts of generosity as proof of his personal indifference to money. All the same, his reputation as a miser persisted.' Avarice is of course the stock charge against Vespasian; it is the only respect in which he fell short of the republican ideal of Tacitus-prorsus, si avaritia abesset, antiquis ducibus par (Hist. 2. 5). Suetonius' conclusions on the subject seem to be sound enough; that the condition of Roman finances made it imperative for Vespasian to raise money by every means in his power, and that at heart he was a generous man, but that what could fairly be objected to was the fact that some of his methods were ignoble in the extreme, and more fitted to a moneylender than to an emperor.

p.note: . Galba had a reputation for parsimony second only to Vespasian (Suet. Galb. 12), but we have evidence to show that he allowed some tribute-reduction to Spain and Gaul, the provinces that had made him emperor. The words of Tacitus, Galliae obligatae in posterum tributi levamento (Hist. 1. 8), are illustrated by by Gallic and Spanish coinissues of Galba with the legend Quadragensuma remissa (probably meaning the 20 per cent. portorium tax; see Mattingly, Coins of the Roman Empire in the British Museum, vol. i, e.g. Plate 58, no. 7): no doubt this was one of the taxes that Vespasian reimposed. We know, however, of one case where he allowed a benefit granted by previous emperors to stand: in the Letter to the Vanacinians (Corsica) of 4th October 78 (?) (CIL. x. 8038), he writes: Beneficia tributa vobis ab divo Augusto post septimum consulatum, quae in tempora Galbae retinuistis, confirmo.

. Similarly Dio (66. 8), speaking of Vespasian at Alexandria: πολλὰ δὲ καὶ τέλη τὰ μέν τινα ἐκλελειμμένα ἀνενεώσατο, τὰ δὲ καὶ νομιζόμενα προσεπηύξησε, καινά τε ἕτερα προσκατε- στήσατο, τὸ δ᾽ αὐτὸ τοῦτο καὶ ἐν τῇ ἄλλῃ ὑπηκόῳ τῇ τε Ἰταλίᾳ καὶ αὐτῇ τῇ ῾Ῥώμῃ μετὰ ταῦτα ἐποίησεν. Very little information is preserved about new taxes imposed by Vespasian; we know, however, of the vectigal urinae (see on c. 23). As for fresh tributes levied in the provinces, there is the fiscus Iudaicus, which was merely the appropriation to the Capitoline temple of the tax paid previously by all Jews to the temple at Jerusalem (Dio 66.7; Jos. B. I. 7. 6. 6), and hardly comes under this category. To Vespasian's reign also have been dated the fiscus Asiaticus and the fiscus Alexandrinus, about which we know for certain only that they were administered from Rome by imperial freedmen. Probably they were both taxes collected by a particular levy and paid into a special fund at Rome, and the fiscus Alexandrinus may plausibly be connected with the arrangements for the corn-supply from Egypt (Tac. Hist. 4. 52; see Hirschfeld, Kaiserliche Verwaltungsbeamten², pp. 71 sq. and 370 sq.).

div.p: § 2. ne candidatis quidem... cunctatus est. Dio alludes to this practice (66. 14) as carried on through the agency of Vespasian's mistress Caenis. He adds that it resulted in leniency to the guilty, but never in injustice to the innocent, ἀπέκτεινε μὲν γὰρ Οὐεσπασια- νὸς χρημάτων ἕνεκα οὐδένα, ἔσωσε δὲ πολλοὺς τῶν διδόντων.

p.note: . It is hard to believe this story, which Suetonius qualifies with creditur. In our scanty records of Vespasian's reign there is only one possible case of a provincial officer being accused of extortion, - C. Iulius Bassus, apparently as quaestor of Bithynia, and he was acquitted (Plin. Ep. 4. 9).

div.p: §3. negata sibi gratuita libertate. For a slave might buy his freedom out of money saved from his peculium, if his master was willing to sell (cf. Tac. Ann. 14. 42, suggested reason for assassination of Pedanius Secundus).

p.note: , non mores. We can understand what was meant by these accusations against Vespasian of introducing into public life the shadier methods of enrichment, when we remember that he had been convicted while a privatus of obtaining the latus clavus for a young man, and exacting a reward for his services (c. 4).

. One of Vespasian's most oppressive measures was his appropriation and sale of subseciva, pieces of land left unassigned on the foundation of a colony and subsequently occupied by squatters, some of whom had enjoyed a tenure, illegal though it undoubtedly was, for generations. But this ancient application of nullum tempus occurrit Regi proved so exceptionally unpopular-deputations from all parts of Italy, we are told, in. veighed against it-that Vespasian was compelled to give up this method of enriching the fiscus, though confiscations already made were not annulled (Frontinus de contr. agr. in Gromatici veteres, i, p. 54). •

. The immense sum named, 40,000,000,000 HS., shows that there was ample justification for Vespasian's alarm and remedial methods. It is interesting to find that arrangements were made to raise a State loan of 60,000,000 HS. from private investors, but the system was strange to Roman finance and was abandoned (Tac. Hist. 4. 47).

. This, the preliminary qualification for a senatorial career, had been fixed by Augustus at 1,000,000 HS. (Dio 54. 17). Senators unable to make up this sum, however, were often helped by the emperor out of his private purse (Tac. Ann. 1. 75).

div.p: § 1. Marcelliani theatri. This was the theatre built by Augustus in honour of his nephew and son-in-law Marcellus, who had been regarded as his heir, but died prematurely in 23 B. C. (Suet. Aug. 29; Dio 53. 30).

p.note: . The word is applied either to public entertainments, as here, or to private entertainments, such as were given by Trajan to amuse his guests at dinner (Plin. Ep. 6. 31). The point here is clearly that they had been given up for reasons of economy, and that Vespasian showed his generosity by reviving them.

Bücheler has proposed that the name should read Apellae, and the tragoedus be identified with Apelles, a celebrated tragic actor in the reign of the emperor Gaius (Suet. Cal. 33; Dio 59. 5; Petr. 64). This, however, would extend Apelles' life to a somewhat unusual length, and the words of Plocamus in Petronius,-Quando parem habui nisi unum Apelletem?-seem to imply that this Apelles was dead at the time when the Satyricon was written (before 66).

div.p: § 2. Alexandrini Cybiosacten... sordium. See Dio (66. 8) for further particulars of Vespasian's unpopularity at Alexandria during his residence there. The original Cybiosactes (MSS. here give Cybiotanten and must be corrected from Strabo) was a soidisant Seleucid, whom Berenice, daughter and successor to Ptolemy XIII Auletes, had married and associated with her on the throne (55 B. C.); a few days later, however, she had him murdered, οὐ φέρουσα τὸ βάναυσον καὶ τὸ ἀνελεύθερον (Strabo 17.796; see also Dio 39. 57). Κυβιοσάκτης seems to mean 'dealer in salt fish'. Another similar taunt against Vespasian was ἓξ ὀβολοὺς προσαιτεῖς (Dio 66. 8. One would imagine this refers to the fiscus Alexandrinus, on which see on c. 16).

p.note: . Very probably this is the Cerylus of Martial's epigram (1.67): 'Liber homo es nimium, dicis mihi, Ceryle, semper. In te qui dicit, Ceryle, liber homo est. The second line proposed by Ed. Wagner, in te quis dicit, Ceryle, 'liber homo es'? (i. e. 'I am too free, you say: well, no one could say that of you!'), would make the identification with this freedman almost certain. The point of Suetonius' story is that, in Roman law, the master was the heir of his childless freedmen; the estate of Cerylus (who must have been an imperial freedman) would thus revert on his death to Vespasian. Cerylus, to evade the law, had changed his name to Laches and was masquerading as a citizen of free status, and Vespasian's quotation was to show that he had detected the trick, and that the man on his death would be treated as Cerylus, not as Laches. The words come from the Θεοφορουμένη of Menander (quoted at 3236 length in Stobaeus, Flor. 106. 8, fr. 223 Kock), from a passage dealing with reincarnation : Εἴ τις προσελθών μοι θεῶν λέγοι “ Κράτων, ἐπὰν ἀποθάνῃς, αὖθις ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἔσει· ἔσει δ᾽ ὅ τι ἂν βούλῃ, κτλ.”

The following table shows her descent from Augustus (entirely on the female side) : Augustus M. Agrippa Julia L. Aemilius Paullus = Julia M. Silanus (cos. A. D. 19) Aemilia Lepida (Augusti proneptis, Iunia Calvina. Suet. Claud. 26). She was married in 48 or shortly before to L. Vitellius, younger brother of the future emperor (Tac. Ann. 12. 4), but in 49 was relegated (ib. 12. 8) in consequence of an accusation against her of incest with her brother Lucius, the prospective son-in-law of Claudius, and therefore an obstacle to Agrippina's dynastic schemes; on this pretext his betrothal to Octavia was annulled, and no doubt Calvina's marriage also, for in 69 we find L. Vitellius married to Triaria (ib. Hist. 2. 63). Calvina's relegatio was repealed by Nero in 59 as a political measure against his mother's memory (ib. Ann. 14. 12). This is the lady whom Racine (rather absurdly) made the heroine of his Britannicus.

. This, of course, in reference to his imminent apotheosis (see also Dio 66. 17). As a matter of fact he was deified immediately after his death, as many inscriptions of the year 79 testify (e.g. CIL. iii. 6732, x. 6812). A temple to Divus Vespasianus was erected before 87 (Acta Arv., Henzen, p. cxvii), and his worship was celebrated therein, entrusted to the charge of a college of fifteen members, the Sodales Flaviales, called also Titiales after the death and deification of Titus. That Vespasian, in spite of his dislike for fictitious honours, was well aware of the political value of the cult of the Divine Emperor, is shown by the establishment during his reign of concilia for Caesar-worship, not only in the newly-acquired Agri Decumates at Arae Flaviae, but in some of the less backward provinces that previous emperors had left untouched: Africa. Later sacerdotes give their order in the lists, and the first sacerdos can thus be dated approximately to 71-73 (see McElderry in J. R. S. 1913, p. 122). Baetica. The flamen Augustalis in Baetica primus is mentioned in an inscription (CIL. ii. 3271): from the other offices this man held we can date his flamonium to early in Vespasian's reign. The genuineness of the inscription has, however, been questioned (see McElderry in J. R. S. 1918, p. 82). Gallia Narbonensis. An inscription of Q. Trebellius Rufus (CIA. iii. 623-4) calls him ἀρχιερεὺς πρῶτος ἐπαρχείας τῆς ἐκ Ναρβῶνος. This man was later archon at Athens, an office that can be dated to Domitian's reign (see Graindor, Rev. Arch. July 1917, p. 17 sq.): his sacerdotium may then plausibly be placed under Vespasian. This, of course, means that the famous inscription dealing with the concilium provinciae Narbonensis (CIL. xii. 6038 = Dessau 6964), supposed to be Augustan, must be assigned to the reign of Vespasian. On the revival of the cult of Divus Claudius see note on c. 9.

p.mentioned: extinctus est VIIII. Kal. Iul. septimum
p.note: : i. e. on 23rd June, 79. He was born on 17th November, A. D. 9. (c. 2), so that Suetonius' 69 years 7 months 7 days for the length of his life is a correct reckoning (septimum to be taken with mensem as well as with diem), since the Romans included both terminal dates in their calculations. But there is some dispute as to the date of his death, owing to the conflicting statements of Dio, who says (66. 17), ἔζησε δὲ ἔτη ἐννέα καὶ ἑξήκοντα καὶ μῆνας ὀκτώ, to which Zonaras adds, καὶ ἡμέρας ὀκτώ. This is obviously wrong, but it has been suggested that the original text of Dio read, καὶ μῆνας ἑπτὰ καὶ ἡμέρας ὀκτώ, i. e. date of death 25th June, making Dio calculate exclusively, as an exclusive calculation makes his next statement, ἐμονάρχησε δὲ ἔτη δέκα ἡμερῶν ἐξ δέοντα, support the same date. On the whole, Suetonius seems most likely to be right, even if the text of Dio were absolutely clear: many modern writers, however (e.g. Weynand in Pauly-Wissowa), give the date as 24th June, apparently as a compromise. (The length given for the reign of Titus-who died on 13th September 81- i. e. 2 years 2 months 20 days, Suet. Tit. II; Dio 66. 26, certainly fixes the starting-point at 24th or 25th June, but is no evidence at all that Vespasian died on the same day.) Dio (66. 17), mentions, only to deny, a rumour that Vespasian was poisoned by Titus: he says this was believed by the emperor Hadrian among others. It is rather strange that Suetonius omitted to record this, if it was really a favourite theory at court in his time.

. The only one known to us is the conspiracy in 79 of A. Caecina Alienus and T. Clodius Eprius Marcellus (Dio 66. 16; Suet. Tit. 6; the date is clear because the conspiracy is recorded by Dio as contemporaneous with the execution of Iulius Sabinus, and that this took place in 79 we know from Tac. Hist. 4. 67). These two men, one the old Vitellian general, the other the famous orator, were both trusted friends of Vespasian. It was obviously to be a military rebellion, for Caecina was apprehended through the discovery by Titus of a chirographum eius praeparatae apud milites contionis (Suet. loc. cit.), but our other details deal entirely with the mode of death of the two conspirators. We may perhaps detect the signs of other coniurationes in the suspectissimus quisque against whom Titus as praefectus praetorio took precautions (Suet. loc. cit.).

p.mentioned: aut filios sibi successuros aut neminem
p.note: : i. e. Vespasian's horoscope showed so unmistakably that no one else would succeed him. There does not seem the slightest reason for imagining that this famous remark implies qualified republican sympathies. For Dio's use of it (66. 12) see note on c. 15. We may note, with regard to the succession, that Vespasian, in spite of his confidence, left nothing to chance. From the very beginning of the reign everything was done to make the accession of Titus, and of Domitian after him, as certain and smooth as possible. Titus became Caesar and princeps iuventutis (titles reserved for heirs of the imperial house) before the end of 69; later, he was his father's colleague in the censorship and in seven eponymous consulships (see on c. 8); he received the tribunicia potestas from Ist July, 71 (when Vespasian became trib. pot. III); he was saluted as imperator on the occasion of the Jewish triumph in 71 (see on c. 8), and thenceforward his salutations and his father's are concurrent; &c. It is clear, however, that Titus was not regarded as an equal sharer in his father's imperial powers: this point, though not strictly relevant, may perhaps be briefly considered here. There is literary evidence to suggest that during Titus' stay in the East, there was friction between the father and the son with regard to Titus' position in the empire (Suet. Tit. 5), and we know that Titus allowed coins to be issued in the East giving him the praenomen Imperatoris, and accepted the salutation as imperator from the troops on the occasion of the fall of Jerusalem, though technically he was only his father's legatus. It is this, no doubt, that explains the passage of Philostratus, who says of Titus 'Αναρρη- θεὶς δ᾽ αὐτοκράτωρ ἐν τῇ ῾Ῥώμῃ καὶ ἀριστείων ἀξιωθεὶς τούτων ἀπῄει μὲν ἰσομοιρήσων τῆς ἀρχῆς τῷ πατρί (Apoll. 6. 30). But on Titus' return to Rome, we see clearly that the praenomen Imperatoris was definitely withheld from him, though in one coin-issue of 71 he is apparently described as designatus Imperator. His customary official title on the senatorial bronze is T. Caesar Vespasianus Imp. (with or without the number of salutations), and on the gold and silver T. Caesar Imp. Vespasianus: in either case the title Imperator is used as a cognomen only. (The use of the praenomen Imperatoris, which occurs on coins and in inscriptions, mostly from the eastern provinces, throughout the reign, is therefore technically incorrect.) Vespasian thus retained the exclusive right to the praenomen Imperatoris, as well as to the title Augustus, and this proves that Titus' position was definitely subordinate. (See, for a survey of the evidence, Weynand in Pauly-Wissowa, vi. 2708 sq. : the coin-issues of Vespasian's reign are described in Mattingly's article 'The Mints of Vespasian' in Numismatic Chronicle, 1921, p. 187 sq.) To secure Domitian's position was not of course a matter of such urgency, though since Titus was without male issue, it was presumed and arranged that he would eventually succeed. He also received the titles Caesar and princeps iuventutis before the end of 69, was consul six times during his father's reign (once ord., five times suff.), became a member of all the priestly colleges, &c. His official title during the reign was Caesar Aug. f. Domitianus. Vespasian, it seems clear, expected that Titus on his accession would give Domitian the same position as he had held himself under his father, but Titus, for whatever reason, did not, and Domitian never received either the tribunicia potestas or the title Imperator during his brother's reign. Nevertheless, he was obviously always regarded as his brother's successor.
